passage: Throughout this work we convert gas-phase oxygen abundances into units of solar metallicity assuming a solar value of 12+log(O/H)_sun = 8.69, following the recent photospheric determination based on 3D hydrodynamical model atmospheres with non-LTE corrections. This corresponds to an oxygen mass fraction X_O of roughly 0.0057 and a total solar metallicity Z_sun = 0.0134. Adopting the older value of 8.83 would lower all of our inferred metallicities by about 0.14 dex, whereas the 8.73 value favoured by some calibrations changes them by only 0.04 dex. Direct-method abundances at 12+log(O/H) = 7.7, for example, correspond to Z ~ 0.1 Z_sun under our assumed normalization. We note that the choice of solar scale does not alter relative comparisons between samples.

An ionized, spherically symmetric stellar wind of constant velocity produces a characteristic free-free spectrum with flux density S_nu proportional to nu^0.6 in the radio and infrared, as shown by the classic Wright and Barlow analysis. The flux density scales as S_nu ∝ (Mdot / v_inf)^(4/3) nu^0.6 d^-2 for fixed wind temperature, so that the emission is far more sensitive to mass-loss rate than to terminal velocity. For a Wolf-Rayet star with Mdot = 3x10^-5 Msun/yr and v_inf = 2000 km/s at a distance of 2 kpc, we expect ~1 mJy at 5 GHz. The optically thick photosphere radius grows toward lower frequencies, so that radio emission arises at much larger radii than the near-infrared excess. Clumping inflates the inferred Mdot by a factor f_cl^(1/2).

Combining the temperature and polarization power spectra with CMB lensing, the final Planck data release yields tight constraints on the six parameters of the base flat LambdaCDM model. We find a Hubble constant H0 = 67.4 +/- 0.5 km/s/Mpc and a matter density parameter Omega_m = 0.315 +/- 0.007, with Omega_b h^2 = 0.0224, Omega_c h^2 = 0.120, spectral index n_s = 0.965 +/- 0.004 and optical depth tau = 0.054 +/- 0.007. The amplitude of fluctuations is sigma_8 = 0.811 +/- 0.006. The inferred H0 lies about 4 to 5 sigma below local distance-ladder measurements using Cepheid-calibrated supernovae, a tension that persists when adding baryon acoustic oscillation data, which pull H0 only marginally higher.

We estimate gas-phase oxygen abundances using the strong-line calibration derived from direct T_e-based measurements of local analogs of high-redshift galaxies, namely extreme emission-line systems selected from SDSS with auroral [O III] 4363 detections and high specific star formation rates. The R3 index, log([O III]5007/Hbeta), is fit with a cubic polynomial in x = 12+log(O/H) - 8, with an intrinsic scatter of about 0.1 dex. Because R3 is double-valued, peaking near 12+log(O/H) ~ 8.0, we break the degeneracy using [N II]/Halpha or R23 where available. This calibration, applicable over 7.2 < 12+log(O/H) < 8.4, better reproduces the ionization conditions of z > 2 star-forming galaxies than calibrations anchored on local H II regions or photoionization models.

The strong- and weak-lensing mass models for the CLASH clusters are described in detail in a companion analysis of the full sample of 25 massive clusters observed with HST. Multiple-image systems were identified in the 16-band ACS and WFC3 imaging and confirmed with spectroscopic redshifts from VLT/VIMOS, where available, and with photometric redshifts otherwise. Table 2 lists the position, redshift and quality grade of each system, typically 5 to 20 per cluster, with up to 100 images in the best-constrained fields. Parametric models include cluster-scale dark matter halos plus perturbations from individual cluster members scaled with a Faber-Jackson relation, while free-form models are also provided. Weak-lensing shear catalogs from Subaru Suprime-Cam extend the mass maps beyond the Einstein radius to the virial region.

Large-volume hydrodynamical simulations differ markedly in their predicted black hole populations at low stellar mass. At M_* < 10^10 Msun, Illustris and SIMBA produce black holes that are over-massive by up to an order of magnitude relative to the local M_BH-M_* relation extrapolated from dynamical measurements, while TNG300 and EAGLE tend to retain very small black holes, which remain close to their seed mass of ~10^5 Msun h^-1 owing to efficient supernova feedback suppressing accretion. The resulting black hole occupation fractions differ substantially between suites, so comparisons with dwarf-galaxy AGN samples remain inconclusive. Results are sensitive to the seeding prescription, the Bondi boost factor, and the adopted radiative and kinetic feedback efficiencies.

Using NIRCam wide-field slitless grism spectroscopy of quasar fields, we identify broad-line Halpha emitters at 5 < z < 7 among the full sample of several hundred Halpha line emitters. We find that about 10 per cent of Halpha emitters with L_Halpha > 10^42.5 erg/s display broad components with FWHM > 1000 km/s. The corresponding number density is ~10^-5 to 10^-4 cMpc^-3 at M_UV ~ -19 to -21, which is roughly two orders of magnitude higher than the extrapolation of the UV-selected quasar luminosity function. After completeness corrections for the grism sensitivity and line-flux limits, the broad-line AGN fraction among line emitters is 0.8 per cent per magnitude of Halpha luminosity, with large Poisson uncertainties.

The absence of high-ionization lines such as He II 1640, C IV 1549 and N V 1240 in the rest-frame UV spectra of JWST broad-line AGN is puzzling given their strong Balmer emission. Several explanations are possible. A very soft ionizing continuum, with a big blue bump peaking at lower energy than in typical quasars, would reduce the supply of photons above 54 eV needed for He II. Alternatively, very high gas densities (n_H > 10^10 cm^-3) and large column densities in the broad-line region thermalize the emission and suppress collisionally excited UV lines relative to Balmer lines. Low metallicity, Z < 0.1 Z_sun, further weakens C IV and N V. Dense gas can also absorb or scatter the line photons, leading to Balmer breaks and absorption features.

We present an autonomous agent powered by a large language model that interprets multi-band galaxy photometry through iterative spectral energy distribution fitting. Given photometry from HST and JWST NIRCam bands, the agent proposes a physical model (stellar population, star formation history, dust attenuation, nebular emission), calls a fitting code such as Prospector or Bagpipes as a tool, inspects the residuals and posterior corner plots, and revises the model parameterization in a loop until the chi-squared and physical plausibility criteria are satisfied. In tests on 200 mock galaxies with known properties, the agent recovers stellar masses to within 0.15 dex and star formation rates to 0.3 dex, comparable to fits tuned by human experts, while requiring on average 4 iterations per source.

We compare the broad Halpha and Hbeta profiles of the strongly lensed little red dot at z~7 across multiple images, whose differing light-travel delays sample the source over several decades in the rest frame, from about 1990 to the present. The broad Balmer lines, with FWHM ~ 3000 km/s, show no significant change in flux or width over this baseline, with variations below 10 per cent, apart from small shifts in the depth of the narrow Balmer absorption. The lack of long-term variability is in tension with expectations from standard AGN accretion disks, in which broad lines respond to continuum changes with lags of weeks to years, and suggests either a massive black hole with a large broad-line region or a dense, optically thick gas envelope that smooths variations.

We model the early-time spectra of the kilonova AT2017gfo using a P Cygni profile formalism, with the line source function in the Sobolev approximation. The broad absorption features at 1 micron, centered at velocities of 0.2c to 0.3c in the first few days, are reproduced by Sr II in a lanthanide-poor outflow. The emission component of each P Cygni profile is weak or absent in some epochs, which implies an ejecta that is photospheric and aspherical. Fits with a spherically symmetric, expanding photosphere yield a velocity of 0.28c at 1.5 days that declines to 0.17c at 3.5 days; the line profile shape can be matched only with an asymmetric ejecta geometry viewed at an inclination near the polar axis, with an axis ratio of ~1.5.

In the EAGLE simulations the specific star formation rate of star-forming central galaxies declines with stellar mass, from sSFR ~ 10^-9.5 yr^-1 at M_* = 10^9 Msun to 10^-10.3 yr^-1 at 10^11 Msun at z = 0. This trend arises because higher-mass halos accrete gas at a lower specific rate, and because feedback from AGN, which is more efficient in massive halos with large central black holes, heats the circumgalactic medium and reduces the gas supply. Mass-dependent gas fractions also reduce the star formation efficiency at fixed gas surface density, since a larger fraction of the baryons is locked up in the stellar component and in the hot halo. The decline steepens at M_* > 10^10.5 Msun where quenching begins.

Several cosmological simulations have identified atomic-cooling halos with T_vir > 10^4 K at z ~ 15 that grow rapidly, with halo masses of ~10^8 Msun and accretion rates of order 0.1 to 1 Msun/yr onto the central gas cloud. In these halos, a Lyman-Werner background of J_21 > 100 or violent merger-driven turbulence prevents molecular hydrogen cooling and fragmentation, and gas collapses isothermally at ~8000 K. Resolution of the inner parsec shows a supermassive star of 10^4 to 10^5 Msun forming through rapid accretion, which could directly collapse into a black hole. Zoom-in radiation hydrodynamics simulations and N-body plus semi-analytic models both indicate that such halos are rare, with number densities below 10^-6 cMpc^-3.

We select little red dot candidates using a pair of color criteria that isolate the V-shaped spectral energy distribution across a wide range of redshifts. A red optical slope is required, F277W - F444W > 1.5 mag for sources at z ~ 5 to 8, with the filter pair shifted to F200W - F356W at lower redshift, while a blue UV slope is enforced with F115W - F150W < 0.8 mag. Compactness is required through a half-light radius below 0.2 arcsec and a ratio of aperture fluxes consistent with a point source. Sources are required to have SNR > 5 in the long-wavelength bands. Photometric redshifts from EAZY, excluding brown dwarfs through a stellar template fit, give a sample of several hundred candidates with a contamination rate of about 15 per cent.

Recent work has introduced autonomous agents based on large language models for the interpretation of JWST galaxy spectral energy distributions. In such frameworks, the agent explores a space of physical models, such as stellar population, dust and AGN components, via Monte Carlo tree search, where each node represents a model configuration, expansion corresponds to adding or modifying a component, and rewards are given by the Bayesian information criterion and physical priors. The LLM proposes branch candidates, runs the fitting code, and reads the results to evaluate the next steps. Applied to NIRCam photometry of 500 high-redshift galaxies, the tree search converged on a preferred model for 90 per cent of sources, and recovered the correct number of components in mock tests with 85 per cent accuracy.

When a star is tidally disrupted by a massive black hole, roughly half of the stellar debris is bound and returns at a rate that peaks well above the Eddington value. In this regime, the returning debris is thought to form a radiation-pressure-supported, quasi-spherical envelope of radius ~10^14 to 10^15 cm, which reprocesses the accretion luminosity of the inner disk. The envelope radiates near the Eddington luminosity L ~ 10^44 erg/s at an effective temperature of ~3x10^4 K, so that the optical emission is blue, smooth and long-lived, with a nearly constant color and a slow decline. The emission is bright in the optical and UV but weak in X-rays, which are absorbed and reprocessed by the thick envelope unless viewed along the polar axis.

Our simulations adopt a spatially uniform, redshift-dependent metagalactic radiation field that includes ultraviolet and X-ray photons produced by galaxies and quasars. The background is taken from a recent synthesis model that integrates the observed galaxy UV luminosity function and quasar luminosity function, with an assumed escape fraction of ionizing photons of 20 per cent for galaxies, and propagates the radiation through an intergalactic medium opacity computed from the observed column density distribution of absorbers. The resulting photoionization and photoheating rates for H I, He I and He II are tabulated as functions of redshift from z = 0 to 15, and are applied as an optically thin background, with self-shielding at n_H > 10^-2 cm^-3 following a fitting function. Hydrogen reionization completes at z ~ 6.

Radio observations offer a potentially powerful discriminant between physical models for little red dots. If the red continuum is powered by a standard AGN with a relativistic jet, we expect radio luminosities of L_5GHz ~ 10^40 to 10^42 erg/s, detectable in deep VLA or MeerKAT imaging. In contrast, an envelope of dense gas that surrounds a rapidly accreting, super-Eddington black hole would absorb emission by free-free absorption and synchrotron self-absorption, giving rise to radio quietness. Stacking of 500 LRDs in 3 GHz VLA data yields no detection to a 3-sigma limit of 0.3 microJy, corresponding to a radio loudness R < 1, which disfavors jet-dominated scenarios and models in which star formation rates exceed 10^3 Msun/yr.

We construct empirical point spread function models for the JWST Mid-Infrared Instrument imager using dithered observations of bright, isolated stars in the standard calibration field. For each of the nine imaging filters from F560W to F2550W, the PSF is built on a 4x oversampled grid by fitting the stacked, undersampled stellar images, accounting for the sub-pixel phase and the cruciform artifact at shorter wavelengths. Astrometry is calibrated against Gaia DR3 positions, giving a distortion solution with residuals below 0.02 arcsec rms, and absolute photometric zero points are derived from observations of A dwarfs and solar analogs, accurate to 2 to 3 per cent. The ratio of the PSF full width at half maximum to the pixel scale of 0.11 arcsec varies from 1.8 to 7.

We identify a sample of broad-line Green Pea galaxies at z ~ 0.1 to 0.3 from SDSS as potential low-redshift analogs of little red dots. These compact galaxies display strong [O III] emission with equivalent widths above 500 Angstroms, together with broad Halpha components with FWHM of 1000 to 2500 km/s. Their spectral energy distributions show a turnover near 4000 Angstroms and a red optical continuum, resembling the V-shaped SED of high-redshift LRDs, and some display Balmer absorption features. The inferred black hole masses of 10^6 to 10^7 Msun, with Eddington ratios near unity, are consistent with those of LRDs, although the X-ray weakness and the lack of variability remain to be tested with follow-up. The number density of ~10^-6 Mpc^-3 is far lower than the LRD density.

Primordial black holes with a broad, near-critical mass spectrum can account for both the nanohertz gravitational wave background reported by pulsar timing arrays and the abundant massive black holes seen in little red dots. A primordial curvature power spectrum with an enhanced amplitude at k ~ 10^6 Mpc^-1 produces scalar-induced gravitational waves with a spectral peak at nanohertz frequencies, requiring a primordial black hole abundance of f_PBH ~ 10^-3 at masses near solar-mass scales. In this scenario, a subset of PBHs, clustered within dark matter halos, would grow through accretion and mergers to 10^6 to 10^7 Msun by z ~ 7. Such seeds naturally yield overmassive black holes relative to the host galaxies, but the model is constrained by X-ray background and CMB limits on accretion.

We report the discovery of an X-ray luminous, radio-loud quasar at z = 3.4 identified in the eFEDS field observed with eROSITA. The source has a 0.5-2 keV rest-frame luminosity of 10^46 erg/s, with a spectral index Gamma = 2.3, and a radio-loudness parameter R ~ 200 from LOFAR and VLA data. The spectral energy distribution and a single-epoch virial black hole mass estimate from the Mg II line, M_BH ~ 10^9 Msun, yield a bolometric luminosity corresponding to an Eddington ratio lambda_Edd ~ 1.5, indicating that this source is accreting at or above the Eddington limit. The soft X-ray spectrum and the strong Fe II emission are consistent with a high accretion rate, as is the blueshifted C IV emission.

We fit the emission line complexes of AGN spectra using a Bayesian spectral decomposition code. The software models the continuum as a power law plus host galaxy template and the Fe II pseudo-continuum, with each emission line complex such as Halpha plus [N II] 6548,6584 and [S II] 6717,6731 described as a sum of Gaussian or Gauss-Hermite components for narrow, intermediate and broad profiles. Posterior distributions are sampled with nested sampling, which provides the Bayesian evidence for model comparison, for example to determine whether an additional broad component is statistically justified. The code is applied to SDSS-type optical spectra with signal-to-noise > 10 per pixel and returns line fluxes, FWHM, and black hole mass estimates with proper propagation of uncertainties.

Our cosmological simulations were performed with the moving-mesh hydrodynamics code AREPO. The code solves the equations of ideal magnetohydrodynamics on an unstructured Voronoi mesh that moves with the fluid flow, using a second-order unsplit Godunov scheme with an exact or HLLD Riemann solver. This provides a quasi-Lagrangian approach to hydrodynamics that is, unlike fixed-grid codes, Galilean invariant, which means that the solution does not depend on the bulk velocity of the fluid and avoids advection errors. Gravity is computed with a TreePM algorithm, with the tree for short-range forces and a particle-mesh method for long-range forces. The mesh-generating points are regularized to maintain cell shapes, and cells are refined and derefined to keep masses within a factor of two of the target mass.

We consider several physical explanations for the extreme F356W-dropout source, which is detected only at wavelengths longer than 4 microns. A galaxy at z ~ 30 with a Lyman break redshifted to 3.6 microns would imply an implausibly early assembly with a stellar mass above 10^9 Msun, in conflict with LambdaCDM predictions, and is disfavored by the lack of a nearby non-detection in F277W, and by a Lyman-alpha forest with a low probability. A cool brown dwarf of spectral type T or Y, at a distance of a few hundred parsecs in the Galactic halo, can reproduce the very red F356W - F444W colour owing to methane absorption, but the source is spatially compact with proper motion consistent with zero. Other options include a heavily obscured AGN or a dusty galaxy at z ~ 6.

If the faint-end slope of the galaxy UV luminosity function steepens with redshift, with alpha evolving from -1.9 at z = 6 to -2.4 at z = 10, then faint galaxies below M_UV = -17 contribute a rising fraction of the total ionizing emissivity. Assuming an escape fraction f_esc = 0.2 and a ionizing photon production efficiency log xi_ion = 25.6 Hz/erg, integrating the luminosity function down to M_UV = -13 yields a Thomson scattering optical depth of tau_e = 0.058, consistent with the CMB measurement of 0.054 +/- 0.007 within 1 sigma. In contrast, truncating the luminosity function at M_UV = -17 gives tau_e = 0.040, in tension with the data. Reionization is then 50 per cent complete at z ~ 7.8, and completes by z ~ 6.

We compare the predicted sizes of disc galaxies from semi-analytic models with the observed size-luminosity distribution of field spirals. In the models, disc scale lengths are calculated assuming that the specific angular momentum of the cooling gas is conserved and that the discs are in centrifugal equilibrium in the dark matter halo, with the halo spin parameter drawn from a lognormal distribution with mean lambda = 0.05. The resulting median half-light radius at a fixed luminosity agrees with the observed relation from SDSS within 0.1 dex over the range -23 < M_r < -17, with a scatter of 0.25 dex, comparable to the observed scatter. The models, however, overproduce the number of compact, low-surface-brightness discs and fail to reproduce the brightest large spirals.

We study the evolution of a massive disk that is fed at a rate of 1 Msun/yr onto a very massive central object of 10^5 Msun, under conditions expected during direct collapse supermassive black hole formation. The disk surface density becomes large enough that the Toomre parameter drops below unity at radii beyond ~0.1 pc, and the disk is expected to fragment. However, our simulations find that at accretion rates above 0.1 Msun/yr, efficient angular momentum transport by spiral density waves and gravitational torques leads to a smooth inflow with only transient clumps that are sheared or accreted. Clumps that form do so with masses of 10 to 100 Msun, and migrate inward on timescales shorter than the Kelvin-Helmholtz time, suppressing the formation of stellar-mass objects.

Decaying supersonic turbulence dissipates kinetic energy more slowly than would be expected for a flow with a fixed driving scale. In a simple picture, the energy decay timescale is the eddy turnover time, t_d ~ L/v, so energy should decay as t^-1 for an isothermal flow. Our simulations instead find E ∝ t^-eta with eta ~ 0.8 to 1.0 at Mach numbers of 5 to 10. The shallower decay arises because the characteristic scale of the flow grows as small-scale structures dissipate in shocks, so that the integral scale increases with time, L ∝ t^0.5. The energy is transferred to larger scales via the merging of shock-compressed density structures, and the compressive modes decay faster than the solenoidal ones, which are damped only by numerical viscosity.

We model the Chandra ACIS point spread function for automated source extraction using a library of ray-traced PSFs generated with the SAO raytrace code and MARX. The PSF depends on off-axis angle, azimuth and photon energy, and we sample it on a grid of 0.5 keV and 1 arcmin steps, interpolating between grid points. Aspect dither, with a Lissajous pattern of amplitude 16 arcsec and periods of 707 and 1000 s, is included by convolving with the exposure-weighted path of the source on the detector, accounting for chip edges and bad pixels. The pixelization of the ACIS detector, 0.492 arcsec per pixel, is incorporated by integrating the model over each pixel. The 90 per cent encircled energy radius, from ~1 arcsec on-axis to > 10 arcsec at 10 arcmin, is used to define extraction regions.

We predict the number of galaxies at z ~ 8 and z ~ 10 detectable in JWST surveys such as JADES and CEERS using extrapolations of the observed UV luminosity function, with a Schechter form with M* = -21 and alpha = -2.1 at z = 8. For JADES Deep, which reaches 5-sigma limits of 30.5 mag in NIRCam filters over 46 arcmin^2, we expect about 300 galaxies at z ~ 8 and about 100 at z ~ 10, while the shallower CEERS survey, covering 100 arcmin^2 with a depth of 29 mag, should yield about 80 galaxies at z ~ 8 and 15 at z ~ 10, after accounting for completeness and cosmic variance, with an uncertainty of 30 per cent from the luminosity function parameters and a drop-out selection efficiency of 70 per cent.

Halpha is a robust tracer of the star formation rate because it is produced by recombination of hydrogen ionized by massive stars with M > 10 Msun and lifetimes under 10 Myr, so it traces the instantaneous star formation rate. The calibration assumes Case B recombination, in which the gas is optically thick to Lyman line photons so that each Lyman photon is absorbed and eventually converted into Balmer photons, with an electron temperature of 10^4 K and a density of 100 cm^-3, which gives an Halpha/Hbeta ratio of 2.86. Every ionizing photon produces 0.45 Halpha photons, with no escape of ionizing photons. Using a Kroupa initial mass function and solar metallicity stellar models, SFR(Msun/yr) = 5.5x10^-42 L(Halpha) in erg/s, with dust corrections from the Balmer decrement.

We select Gaia-Enceladus halo stars from Gaia DR3 using cuts in orbital energy and angular momentum. Stellar positions and velocities are transformed to Galactocentric coordinates, assuming a solar distance of 8.2 kpc and a circular speed of 232 km/s, and the energy is computed in a static axisymmetric potential. Stars are selected with -1.6x10^5 < E < -1.1x10^5 km^2/s^2 and |L_z| < 500 kpc km/s, so as to isolate a radially biased, nearly non-rotating population with high orbital eccentricity above 0.7. We further require a parallax over error of at least 5 and a tangential velocity above 200 km/s to remove disc contaminants. This selection yields about 25,000 stars, with a contamination from in-situ halo stars estimated at around 20 per cent.

We determine the local cosmic stellar mass density from the GAMA survey, using stellar mass estimates obtained from SED fitting to ugriZYJHK photometry. After applying a correction for the evolution of the stellar mass function over the redshift range 0.013 < z < 0.1, the stellar mass function at z = 0 follows a double Schechter form with log M* = 10.78 and a faint-end slope of -1.47. Integrating the function from 10^6 to 10^13 Msun yields a stellar mass density of rho_* = (2.3 +/- 0.2)x10^8 Msun/Mpc^3 (with h = 0.7), corresponding to Omega_* = 0.0017, or a fraction of baryons in stars of about 4 per cent. The uncertainty is dominated by cosmic variance and assumptions about the initial mass function.

We have implemented updated prescriptions for stellar winds and for remnant masses into the direct N-body cluster code NBODY6, replacing the older analytic formulae. To validate the implementation, we compare the initial-to-remnant mass relations for single stars at metallicities from Z = 0.0002 to 0.02 with the output of the standalone binary population synthesis code. For single stars between 0.8 and 150 Msun, the final remnant masses in the N-body code agree with the standalone code to within 1 per cent, including the non-monotonic structure caused by pair-instability and pulsational pair-instability supernovae and the neutron star to black hole transition near 20 Msun. Small differences of a few per cent arise only from the timestep interpolation of the stellar evolution tracks and rapid mass-loss episodes.

We estimate the number of quasars at z > 7 that could be found by a Euclid-like wide survey covering 15,000 deg^2 with limiting magnitude of Y, J, H ~ 24. Assuming that the quasar luminosity function evolves as a double power-law with a steep bright-end slope of -3.5 and a density evolution of 0.5 dex per unit redshift, we predict about 100 quasars at z > 7 and 10 quasars at z > 8, with M_1450 < -25. A sample of this size would constrain the bright end slope and the break luminosity to within 20 per cent, and the quasar number density at z = 7.5 to within 30 per cent, and give strong constraints on seed formation models and on the black hole mass function, constraints that are currently dominated by Poisson noise.

The Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope consists of 30 fully steerable parabolic dishes of 45 m diameter, arranged in a Y-shaped configuration, with 14 antennas in a central compact array within a region of 1 km and the remaining 16 antennas distributed along three arms, giving maximum baselines of about 25 km and minimum baselines of about 100 m. At 150 MHz, the primary beam full width at half maximum is approximately 3.1 degrees, giving a field of view of roughly 7 deg^2, and the angular resolution is about 20 arcsec. The system temperature is around 615 K at 150 MHz, dominated by sky noise from the Galactic synchrotron background, with an antenna gain of 0.33 K/Jy, and the instantaneous bandwidth is 32 MHz.

Stellar feedback plays a central role in regulating the growth of black holes in low-mass galaxies. In our simulations, supernova-driven outflows expel dense gas from the nuclear regions of galaxies with M_* < 10^10 Msun, which keeps black holes under-massive relative to the M_BH-M_bulge relation by up to 1 to 2 dex at z > 2. The gas supply to the black hole is limited, and accretion is intermittent. Once the galaxy reaches a stellar mass near 10^10 Msun, the potential well becomes deep enough that supernova feedback is no longer able to expel the gas, and the black hole enters a phase of rapid, nearly Eddington-limited growth which brings it onto the local scaling relation within about 1 Gyr, after which AGN feedback self-regulates the growth.

We examine how spatial and temporal resolution in stellar evolution models affect the predicted black hole mass at the peak below the pair-instability gap. Using MESA models of massive helium cores, we find that coarse mass-grid and timestep choices can artificially suppress the strength of late-stage shell burning and the final core-collapse outcome, so that the maximum black hole mass shifts by up to 5 Msun. Increasing the number of mass zones from 1000 to 3000 and tightening the time-step control for the carbon and oxygen burning phases moves the predicted peak of the black hole mass distribution from ~40 Msun to ~46 Msun at low metallicity, close to the onset of pulsational pair-instability. Convergence is reached above ~2000 zones, while the uncertainty in the 12C(alpha,gamma)16O rate remains the dominant systematic.

In the deep NIRSpec high-resolution spectrum of the Little Red Dot, the He I 7065 line, observed at 1.06 microns, is detected with a clear, asymmetric profile. A single Gaussian fit gives FWHM ~ 600 km/s, substantially narrower than the broad Halpha component, which has FWHM ~ 2500 km/s, but broader than the forbidden lines. The profile shows a blueshifted absorption trough at about -200 km/s relative to the emission peak, with an equivalent width of ~2 Angstroms, as seen in the He I 10830 and 3889 lines and in the Balmer series. The absorption indicates that dense, metastable He I (2^3S) gas with a column density of ~10^15 cm^-2 lies along the line of sight, consistent with an outflow or a dense gas cocoon surrounding the central source.

We model viscous accretion tori around black holes using general-relativistic viscous hydrodynamics, adopting the relativistic generalization of the Navier-Stokes stress-energy tensor, T^{mu nu} = (rho h) u^mu u^nu + P g^{mu nu} - 2 rho nu sigma^{mu nu}, with the shear tensor sigma^{mu nu} projected orthogonally to the fluid four-velocity. The kinematic shear viscosity is parametrized following the alpha prescription, nu = alpha c_s^2 / Omega_K, where c_s is the sound speed and Omega_K is the local Keplerian angular velocity. We explore values of alpha = 0.01, 0.03 and 0.1, corresponding to viscous timescales of 10 to 100 ms for tori of 0.1 Msun, comparable to the lifetime of a remnant accretion disc after a neutron star merger. The torus is initialised with a constant specific angular momentum Fishbone-Moncrief profile.

Fuzzy (wave) dark matter, composed of an ultralight boson of mass m ~ 10^-22 eV, forms solitonic cores of de Broglie wavelength lambda ~ 1 kpc in galactic halos. Such cores, with radius r_c ∝ M_halo^(-1/3) m^-1, are expected to be below 100 pc in massive cluster halos of M ~ 10^15 Msun, and so cannot account for the kiloparsec-scale dark matter core inferred from strong lensing and stellar kinematics of the central galaxy. Explaining a core of 5 kpc would need a much smaller boson mass of 10^-24 eV, in conflict with Lyman-alpha forest constraints requiring m > 2x10^-21 eV. The mismatch suggests other mechanisms, such as self-interacting dark matter or baryonic feedback, are needed, although tidal interference patterns of fuzzy dark matter may affect lensing.

The blueshift of C IV in luminous quasars at z > 6, which reaches 5000 km/s, is thought to reflect radiation-pressure-driven winds launched from the accretion disc, whose strength is set by the ionizing continuum and the mass accretion rate. We argue that the blueshift should correlate with the mass accreted at the Eddington rate rather than the current black hole mass, since during rapid growth phases the black hole mass lags behind the accretion history. A high accretion rate relative to M_BH, with an Eddington ratio above unity, produces a softer ionizing spectrum, since an extremely thick disc or a slim disc is formed, and a strong wind; and the C IV line is shifted to the blue. The time-integrated mass accreted, rather than the current mass, thus sets the wind kinematics and the observed blueshift.

To study galaxy morphology between z = 3 and 6, we generated mock JWST NIRCam images for 4,500 simulated galaxies drawn from the cosmological hydrodynamical simulation, with stellar masses above 10^9 Msun. For each galaxy, we performed radiative transfer with SKIRT or SUNRISE using stellar population synthesis models and a dust model, along three random lines of sight, producing images in the F115W, F150W, F200W, F277W, F356W and F444W filters. The images are convolved with the empirical PSF, resampled to a pixel scale of 0.03 arcsec, and inserted into blank-field CEERS-like backgrounds with realistic noise. We then measure non-parametric morphological statistics, including Gini, M20, concentration and asymmetry, and Sersic indices, in the same way as for observations.

Using lensed NIRISS slitless spectroscopy of galaxy-cluster fields, we can detect Halpha emitters at z ~ 1 to 2 down to much fainter luminosities than in blank fields. The 5-sigma line flux limit of the F150W and F200W grism observations of 2x10^-18 erg/s/cm^2 over 2 to 3 ks of integration, combined with a typical magnification of mu ~ 5 to 20 in the central regions of the clusters, corresponds to intrinsic Halpha luminosities of L_Halpha ~ 10^39 to 10^40 erg/s at z = 1.5. Such sources have star formation rates of 0.01 Msun/yr and stellar masses below 10^7.5 Msun, which probe the faint end of the Halpha luminosity function and low-mass dwarf galaxies. The source plane completeness falls rapidly for sources with magnification < 2.

To predict the properties of galaxies at z > 10, we build merger trees from a suite of high-resolution N-body simulations with finely spaced snapshots, with 200 outputs between z = 30 and z = 6, corresponding to a time spacing of about 5 Myr at z ~ 10. The simulation follows 2048^3 particles in a box of 100 Mpc/h on a side, giving a particle mass of 10^7 Msun/h, which resolves atomic-cooling halos down to 10^8 Msun. Halos are identified with a friends-of-friends algorithm followed by SUBFIND, and merger trees are built using a subhalo tracking code. The fine time resolution is crucial for capturing the rapid growth and merging of halos at early times and for reducing the numerical noise in semi-analytic predictions of the UV luminosity function and star formation histories.

The incidence of C IV and Si IV absorbers per unit pathlength declines by a factor of 3 to 5 above z ~ 6.5, whereas the incidence of Mg II absorbers remains roughly constant over 2 < z < 7. This behaviour is interpreted as a result of the evolving ionization state of the circumgalactic and intergalactic medium. Mg II traces low-ionization, cool gas in the halos of galaxies, whose covering fraction does not change appreciably, while high-ionization C IV and Si IV require a hard UV background and metal enrichment of the gas at larger distances. At z > 6.5 the metagalactic background is softer and weaker, since reionization is incomplete, and the metals have not yet been transported to large radii by galactic winds, leading to a drop in the C IV comoving mass density, Omega_CIV.

High-resolution ALMA observations show that the [C II] 158 micron emission in z ~ 6 quasar host galaxies extends beyond the bright compact core. Within the central 2 to 3 kpc, [C II] traces a rotating gas disk with dynamical masses of 10^10 to 10^11 Msun, while stacking and deep imaging reveal extended halos of [C II] with radii of 10 to 30 kpc, which contain 10 to 30 per cent of the total line flux. Possible origins include outflows driven by AGN or stellar feedback, which carry metal-enriched gas into the circumgalactic medium, tidal stripping of gas from merging companions, and in-situ star formation in the extended cold-gas reservoirs that feed the quasar. Photoionization by the quasar over such scales is insufficient to explain the surface brightness, and cosmic microwave background attenuation lowers the contrast.

We simulated close encounters and collisions between stellar-mass black holes and main-sequence stars of 100 Msun using smoothed particle hydrodynamics. The black hole masses range from 5 to 50 Msun, and each simulation uses 10^6 particles to model the star. Encounters are parametrized by the impact parameter, ranging from 0 to 3 stellar radii (~ 20 Rsun), and by relative velocities at infinity of 10, 50 and 100 km/s, corresponding to typical velocity dispersions in dense star clusters and nuclear regions. Impacts with b < R_* result in a significant fraction of the stellar mass being captured by the black hole, up to 20 to 50 per cent in the most penetrating cases, while larger impact parameters lead to partial disruption and a bound remnant with tidal tails.

We predict the number of obscured and Compton-thick AGN that SKA radio continuum surveys could detect at high redshift. Assuming that the X-ray luminosity function of AGN evolves with a declining space density at z > 3 and that the radio luminosity correlates with the intrinsic X-ray luminosity, with a fraction of 10 per cent being radio-loud, a SKA1-MID wide survey of 1000 deg^2 reaching a 5-sigma depth of 2 microJy at 1.4 GHz would detect about 10^3 AGN at z > 6, of which ~60 per cent are obscured and about 30 per cent Compton thick, with column densities N_H > 10^24 cm^-2. At z > 10 the numbers decline to a few tens, with large uncertainties dependent on the black hole seeding scenario.

We searched the NIRSpec G395M spectra of the little red dot sample for the Ca II near-infrared triplet at rest-frame 8498, 8542 and 8662 Angstroms, which would reveal an evolved stellar population in the host. In the individual spectra, no significant Ca II triplet absorption is detected, with 3-sigma upper limits on the equivalent width of ~2 Angstroms. The stacked spectrum of 20 LRDs with high S/N shows no absorption at the level of 0.5 Angstroms. Moreover, in the case of the sources with strong Paschen emission, the Ca II triplet is seen in emission, which is a signature of dense gas in the broad-line region with n_H > 10^11 cm^-3, rather than stellar absorption. This suggests that the red continuum is not dominated by old stars.

The O I 8446 emission line is the dominant feature in the 0.8 micron region of the spectra of many quasars with strong Fe II, and arises from Lyman beta fluorescence in the broad-line region. Because of a coincidence between the wavelengths of H I Lyman beta, 1025.72 Angstroms, and the O I 3d 3D - 2p 3P transition at 1025.77 Angstroms, Lyman beta photons are efficiently absorbed by neutral oxygen in the partially ionized zone, and excite the 3d level, which then decays through the 8446 line and the UV 1304 line. The strength of the O I 8446/Halpha ratio, typically 0.05 to 0.1, requires large column densities N_H > 10^23 cm^-2, high densities n_H ~ 10^11 cm^-3 and a large Lyman beta optical depth. The line profile is typically narrower than that of Halpha, thus indicating its origin in an inner dense region.

Among broad-line little red dots with sufficient spectral resolution and S/N, we find that a significant fraction exhibit narrow Balmer absorption features, seen in Halpha, Hbeta and Hgamma, blueshifted or close to the systemic velocity. In the NIRSpec sample of 80 LRDs with R ~ 1000 spectroscopy, 20 sources show clear Halpha absorption at the 3-sigma level, which corresponds to an incidence rate of about 25 per cent, and the fraction rises to about 40 per cent when restricting to the sample with S/N > 20 per resolution element in the continuum. The incidence is much higher than the 1 to 2 per cent rate in typical broad-line quasars, and the equivalent widths of 1 to 10 Angstroms imply hydrogen column densities in the n = 2 level of 10^14 to 10^15 cm^-2.

Constraints on the variability of little red dots are so far limited and generally indicate little or no variability. Multi-epoch NIRCam photometry of several hundred LRDs in the fields JADES, CEERS and COSMOS-Web, with baselines of 1 to 2 years in the observed frame, finds that only about 5 per cent of the sources vary at more than 3-sigma, and most of these are consistent with measurement noise. The structure function amplitude is below 0.05 mag on rest-frame timescales of 100 to 300 days, much lower than that of luminous quasars at comparable luminosities, which show rms variability of 0.1 to 0.2 mag. A few individual sources display broad line equivalent width changes of about 20 per cent. Stacking of the data gives a median variability amplitude of 0.02 +/- 0.01 mag.

Several lines of evidence bear on whether the UV excess of little red dots arises from a star-forming host or the central engine. Evidence for the host includes spatially extended UV emission, offset from the compact red continuum in some sources, with half-light radii of 100 to 300 pc, and UV slopes of beta ~ -2 consistent with young stellar populations with star formation rates of 1 to 10 Msun/yr. Evidence for the AGN includes the broad wings of Mg II and Fe II in the UV, point-like UV morphology in the highest resolution images, UV variability in rare cases, and the lack of a correlation between UV luminosity and stellar mass. The detection of a scattered-light AGN component with a polarization fraction above 5 per cent would also point toward the central engine.

We construct a photometrically selected sample of little red dots from the COSMOS-Web survey using the NIRCam F115W, F150W, F277W and F444W bands together with MIRI F770W where available. Sources are required to be compact (half-light radius below 0.15 arcsec), to show a blue rest-frame UV slope and a red rest-frame optical slope with F277W-F444W > 1.0, and to lie at 4 < z < 8. The resulting catalogue contains roughly 430 candidates over 0.54 deg^2. We stack the photometry in bins of redshift and normalise at rest-frame 1.2 micron, which constrains the average rest-frame near-infrared emission and shows a flat or declining spectrum longward of 1 micron, with no evidence for a hot-dust upturn.

We use the Binary Population and Spectral Synthesis (BPASS) models, version 2.2, which follow the evolution of single and interacting binary stellar populations on a grid of metallicities from Z = 10^-5 to 0.040. Version 2.2.1 provides spectral energy distributions, ionizing photon production rates, supernova rates and remnant numbers for populations with ages from 1 Myr to 100 Gyr, assuming a broken power-law initial mass function with slope -1.3 between 0.1 and 0.5 solar masses and -2.35 above. Binary pathways such as mass transfer, common-envelope evolution and chemically homogeneous evolution produce hotter, longer-lived ionizing sources, and the extended predictions for old stellar populations reproduce the near-infrared colours of evolved systems with ages above 1 Gyr.

High-ionization coronal lines are a defining feature of a subset of narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies. In our sample of 120 NLS1s with SDSS spectra, [Fe VII] lambda6087, [Fe X] lambda6374 and [Fe XI] lambda7892 are detected in 35 per cent of objects, compared with only 8 per cent of broad-line Seyfert 1s. The coronal-line equivalent widths are anticorrelated with Fe II strength: objects with R4570 = Fe II/Hbeta below 0.5 show [Fe X]/[O III] ratios a factor of three higher than strong Fe II emitters. This trend is consistent with a harder, steeper-than-average extreme-ultraviolet ionizing continuum and high Eddington ratios, and with a larger covering factor of gas in the inner narrow-line region at 10-100 pc.

The Millennium-II Simulation follows the evolution of 10 billion dark matter particles in a periodic cubic box of side 100 h^-1 Mpc, a factor of five smaller in length than the original Millennium Run. Each particle has a mass of 6.9 x 10^6 h^-1 solar masses, which is 125 times lower than in the original run, and the gravitational softening length is 1 h^-1 kpc. The adopted cosmology is flat LCDM with Omega_m = 0.25, Omega_Lambda = 0.75, h = 0.73, sigma_8 = 0.9 and n_s = 1. The simulation was run with GADGET-3 from z = 127 to z = 0, with 68 stored snapshots, and haloes resolved with at least 20 particles have masses down to about 10^8 solar masses.

We present a systematic search for intermediate-mass black holes in the local universe using broad Halpha emission in SDSS DR7 spectra. After subtracting the stellar continuum and narrow lines, we identify 305 galaxies at z < 0.35 with a broad component of FWHM between 500 and 2000 km/s, from which virial black hole masses are estimated. The sample has masses in the range 10^5 - 10^6 solar masses, with a median of 1.3 x 10^6, and Eddington ratios of 0.1 to 1. Host galaxies are mostly low-mass, with stellar masses of 10^9 - 10^10 solar masses. X-ray and mid-infrared follow-up confirms AGN activity in about half of the objects, supporting an extension of the black hole mass function to the intermediate-mass regime.

We describe a publicly available code for computing pair counts and two-point correlation functions of simulated haloes or galaxies. The code supports periodic boundary conditions and both auto- and cross-correlations, and computes the three-dimensional correlation function xi(r), the projected function w_p(r_p, pi_max), and the angular correlation function. It uses a cell-linked list with an adaptive grid, vectorised SIMD instructions and OpenMP threading, giving a speedup of a factor of 10-50 over a naive implementation with identical output. For a catalogue of 10^6 objects the pair counts in 20 logarithmic bins from 0.1 to 50 h^-1 Mpc complete in under 10 seconds on a single node with 16 cores. Jackknife covariance estimates are supported.

We investigate the growth of stellar-mass black holes embedded in gas-rich nuclear star clusters. In a cluster with central density above 10^7 solar masses per cubic parsec and a gas reservoir of 10^6 solar masses, a 100 solar mass seed accretes at a Bondi-Hoyle rate that scales as M^2. Because the accretion rate depends on the black hole mass squared, the mass grows faster than exponentially and in the absence of feedback diverges in a finite time, t_div ~ 10 Myr. Mergers with other stellar remnants and stars through runaway collisions further accelerate the growth. Radiative feedback eventually limits the process once the black hole reaches 10^4 solar masses and the accretion rate approaches the Eddington value, and the seeds saturate near 10^4 - 10^5 solar masses by z ~ 10.

We develop a semi-analytic model for the assembly of massive black holes in the early universe, based on dark matter halo merger trees extended to z = 20. Black holes are seeded in haloes through light (100 solar masses) and heavy (10^5 solar masses) channels and grow via Eddington-limited accretion and mergers. We constrain the seed formation efficiency, the accretion duty cycle and the radiative efficiency jointly by two datasets: the amplitude of the nanohertz gravitational wave background measured by pulsar timing arrays, A ~ 2.4 x 10^-15 at f = 1/yr, and the number density and luminosity function of broad-line AGN identified with JWST at z = 4-7. Models reproducing both require heavy seeds or super-Eddington phases, and a high merger-driven background amplitude.

We report the discovery of a population of compact broad-line AGN at z = 4-7 in JWST NIRSpec and NIRCam grism data that exhibit blue UV continua, in contrast to the red optical continua typical of little red dots. Their spectra show broad Halpha components with FWHM of 2000-4000 km/s, rest-frame UV slopes beta ~ -2.2, and compact morphologies with half-light radii below 100 pc. Several show a Balmer break or Balmer absorption in Halpha and Hbeta similar to little red dots, and inferred black hole masses are 10^6.5 - 10^7.5 solar masses. Their X-ray weakness and lack of strong hot-dust emission resemble those of red little red dots, suggesting that they represent a bluer, less obscured extension of the same population.

We study the transfer of Lyman-alpha resonance photons through a static, uniform, optically thick medium using both an analytic solution and Monte Carlo simulation. In a slab or sphere with line-centre optical depth tau_0 > 10^3, photons escape only after scattering into the damping wings, which produces a characteristic double-peaked profile with peaks located at x_p = +/- 0.88 (a tau_0)^(1/3) in Doppler-width units, where a is the Voigt parameter. The double peak is symmetric for a static medium and no flux emerges at line centre. The peak separation scales as N_HI^(1/3) at fixed temperature, and the width of the profile increases with temperature. Partial frequency redistribution in the core and the effect of dust, which preferentially destroys photons with longer path lengths, modify the profiles.

We measure the black hole mass function of broad-line AGN at 3.5 < z < 6 using a JWST sample from NIRCam wide-field slitless spectroscopy in the CEERS and JADES fields. Black hole masses are derived from the broad Halpha line width and luminosity using the local virial relation, yielding masses of 10^6 - 10^8 solar masses. The resulting mass function, corrected for incompleteness, has a number density of about 10^-5 to 10^-4 Mpc^-3 dex^-1 at 10^7 solar masses, which is 10 to 100 times higher than the extrapolation of the bolometric quasar luminosity function. The faint end slope is steep, with alpha ~ -1.5. Compared to local relations, the black holes are overmassive relative to their host stellar masses.

We present new atomic data for [Fe II], including collision strengths computed using the R-matrix method with a large 262-level basis set and Einstein A coefficients from Breit-Pauli calculations. Line ratios among the optical and near-infrared transitions, such as [Fe II] lambda12570 / lambda16440 and lambda8617 / lambda7155, are sensitive to electron density over the range 10^3 - 10^6 cm^-3 and only weakly sensitive to temperature at T = 5000 - 15000 K. The near-infrared ratio lambda12570/lambda16440 varies from 1.35 in the low-density limit to below 1.0 at n_e = 10^5 cm^-3. We compare the resulting diagnostic curves with those based on earlier calculations and with observed spectra of supernova remnants and Herbig-Haro objects.

We examine the relation between continuum shape and hydrogen emission line profile in a sample of 28 spectroscopically confirmed little red dots at z = 4-8. Splitting the sample by the strength of the Balmer break, defined as the ratio of flux density at rest-frame 4200 and 3600 Angstroms, we find that objects with redder continuum slopes and stronger breaks (F_4200/F_3600 > 2) display broader Halpha, with a median FWHM of 3200 km/s compared to 1800 km/s for those with weaker breaks. Exponential rather than Gaussian wings are common, and stacked spectra show extended line wings at the ~1500 km/s level. These trends are consistent with electron scattering in dense gas surrounding the accreting black hole, which broadens the emission lines and imprints the break.

We present a new strong-lensing model of the galaxy cluster Abell 370 (z = 0.375) using JWST NIRCam imaging from the Hubble Frontier Fields follow-up programme and new NIRSpec spectroscopy. Combined with archival HST data, we identify 38 multiply imaged systems comprising 120 images, of which 24 have spectroscopic redshifts. The model has two large-scale dark matter haloes, a bimodal structure, and 270 cluster member galaxies as perturbers, and it reproduces the image positions with a root-mean-square scatter of 0.42 arcsec. The model yields a total mass within 500 kpc of 2.7 x 10^14 solar masses and provides magnification maps, with a median uncertainty of about 10 per cent at magnification mu = 5 for sources at z = 8.

We describe a software package for fitting parametric two-dimensional models to galaxy images. The code decomposes the surface brightness distribution into analytic components, including Sersic, exponential disc, Gaussian, Moffat and Ferrers profiles, each with free centre, ellipticity, position angle and boxy or discy isophote shapes. Models are convolved with a user-supplied point spread function and fitted using a Levenberg-Marquardt minimiser or differential evolution to minimise chi-squared, with a Bayesian version available. The package can handle bad pixel masks and noise images, and writes the best-fit parameters with uncertainties. It is commonly applied to measure the Sersic index, effective radius and bulge-to-total ratio of galaxies in surveys, and to fit a point source plus host galaxy for AGN.

We investigate whether including host galaxy templates improves spectral energy distribution fits for heavily reddened quasars. We fit 150 dust-reddened quasars with E(B-V) = 0.5 - 3 from the UV to the mid-infrared using an AGN template with SMC-like extinction plus a stellar population synthesis model. Adding a host galaxy component reduces the chi-squared substantially for sources with bolometric luminosities below 10^46 erg/s, where the host contributes 20 - 60 per cent of the rest-frame near-infrared flux at 1 micron. At higher luminosities, above 10^47 erg/s, the AGN dominates at all wavelengths and the host is unconstrained. Neglecting the host leads to an overestimate of the reddening by delta E(B-V) ~ 0.3 and of the bolometric luminosity by up to 0.3 dex.

We study the black hole seed mass function predicted by theoretical formation channels in a cosmological context. Rather than a bimodal distribution of light seeds (10 - 100 solar masses from Population III remnants) and heavy seeds (10^4 - 10^5 solar masses from direct collapse), our models predict a continuous spectrum of seed masses spanning 10^2 - 10^6 solar masses. This arises from the range of halo spin, Lyman-Werner flux, metallicity and gas inflow rates, along with runaway stellar collisions in dense clusters, which produce intermediate seeds of 10^3 solar masses. The seed mass function scales roughly as dn/dlogM ~ M^-1 over this range, with the high-mass end truncated by the requirement of metal-free, H2-suppressed haloes. The initial mass thus does not partition cleanly into discrete light and heavy classes.

We show that very dense gas enveloping an accreting black hole can produce the Balmer break and the Balmer absorption features observed in little red dots without invoking an evolved stellar population. Using Cloudy photoionization calculations, we model gas with hydrogen densities of 10^9 - 10^11 cm^-3 and column densities N_H ~ 10^24 cm^-2 illuminated by a quasar continuum. At n = 10^10 cm^-3 a significant population of n = 2 hydrogen builds up through collisional excitation and Lyman-alpha trapping, and bound-free absorption by n = 2 hydrogen yields a break of amplitude F_4200/F_3600 ~ 2 at 3646 Angstroms, together with Balmer absorption lines at Halpha, Hbeta and Hgamma, matching the observed spectra and implying a low stellar mass.

We explore whether dark matter Bondi accretion, aided by the gravitational potential of baryons, can grow black hole seeds quickly enough to explain the abundance of little red dots. A dark matter halo with a cuspy NFW profile and a central baryonic concentration drives a Bondi accretion flow onto a seed of 10^3 - 10^4 solar masses. In the presence of baryonic potential wells the accretion rate increases by a factor of 10 - 100 relative to dark matter alone. For cold or self-interacting dark matter the seeds grow to 10^6 solar masses by z ~ 8, with duty cycle of order unity. The predicted number density of black holes of 10^6 - 10^7 solar masses is about 10^-5 Mpc^-3, consistent with the observed abundance of little red dots.

We analyse the physical properties of 707 submillimetre galaxies in the UKIDSS UDS field, identified with ALMA at 870 micron. Using multiwavelength photometry from the optical to the radio, we derive photometric redshifts, a median of z = 2.6, stellar masses with a median of 10^11 solar masses, star-formation rates of 100 - 500 solar masses per year and dust masses from modified blackbody fits with T_d = 35 K. The 850 micron flux density correlates tightly with the dust mass, M_d ~ S_850^0.9, with a scatter of 0.25 dex, which we attribute to the Rayleigh-Jeans tail of the dust emission being optically thin. At fixed flux, higher-redshift sources have systematically larger dust masses due to the negative K-correction and the increased dust temperature.

We report the detection of microlensing events of individual highly magnified stars in strongly lensed arcs at z = 0.7 - 1.5, behind galaxy cluster lenses observed repeatedly with HST and JWST. Transient point sources are seen near the critical curve, with brightening factors of 0.5 - 2 magnitudes over weeks to months, and magnifications exceeding 1000 for supergiant stars with radii of 10^2 - 10^3 solar radii and effective temperatures of 4000 - 15000 K. Intracluster stars and compact objects with masses of 0.1 - 10 solar masses in the cluster lens create a network of microcaustics that sets the observed rate, about one event per epoch per arc. We compare event rates with simulations and use them to constrain the fraction of dark matter in compact objects.

We predict that the O I lambda8446 and Ca II triplet emission lines arise from the same dense, partially ionized gas in the broad-line region of early massive black holes. In the high-density regime, n_H > 10^10 cm^-3, with ionization parameters log U ~ -2, photoionization models show that O I 8446 is pumped by Lyman-beta fluorescence and Ca II lines form in the same warm neutral zone behind the hydrogen ionization front. The predicted ratio of Ca II lambda8542 to O I lambda8446 is 0.3 - 1, nearly independent of the incident continuum. Both lines should be detectable with JWST NIRSpec in the rest-frame near-infrared of broad-line AGN at z = 5-7 with Halpha FWHM above 2000 km/s, and their velocity widths should closely match one another and the Paschen lines.

We examine the relation between rest-frame UV slope and ionization conditions for 340 galaxies at 4 < z < 9 observed with JWST NIRSpec. Splitting the sample at beta = -2.2, we find that UV-bluer galaxies show higher [O III]5007/[O II]3727 ratios, with a median O32 of 12 compared to 5 for redder objects. The inferred ionization parameter is log U = -2.2 for blue galaxies and -2.7 for red ones. A similar trend appears in [O III]/Hbeta and the equivalent widths of Hbeta. The correlation is consistent with lower dust attenuation, younger stellar populations with less than 10 Myr of age and lower metallicity in bluer galaxies, though the scatter is significant and selection effects at the faint end contribute.

We present a publicly available photometric redshift code that fits spectral energy distribution templates to multi-band galaxy photometry. The code constructs a template grid in redshift, linear combination weights and optional extinction, and finds the best fit by chi-squared minimisation, with the linear coefficients solved analytically at each redshift step. It supports flux upper limits, an apparent-magnitude prior and zero-point offsets, and returns the probability distribution p(z), the 68 per cent confidence interval and the best-fit template. Typical running time is about 10^3 galaxies per second per core, making it suitable for catalogues of 10^7 sources. On the spectroscopic subsample, the normalised median absolute deviation is sigma_NMAD = 0.03 with an outlier fraction of 5 per cent.

The NIRSpec high-resolution spectrum of the little red dot A2744-QSO1 at z = 7.04 resolves the Lyman-alpha emission into distinct narrow and broad components. The narrow component has a FWHM of about 300 km/s, offset by +150 km/s from the systemic velocity measured from [O III] 5007, while a broad component with FWHM of 3500 km/s is detected at lower contrast. After correcting for the magnification of mu = 40, the narrow component dominates the flux, contributing about 80 per cent of the total Lyman-alpha luminosity of 10^43 erg/s, and the broad component carries the remainder. The extended narrow emission, partially resolved in the lensed image, is consistent with scattering in the circumgalactic gas, with the broad component sourced in the broad-line region.

We obtain constraints on the baryon acoustic oscillation distance scale by fitting the galaxy power spectra of the SDSS luminous red galaxy and main samples together with the 2dFGRS. Power spectra are estimated using the optimal quadratic estimator, and a model consisting of a smooth broadband shape times damped oscillations is fitted with a Markov chain Monte Carlo likelihood analysis, marginalising over bias, shot noise and non-linear damping. We evaluate the likelihood as a function of the dilation parameter alpha = D_V/D_V,fid and recover D_V(z = 0.275) / r_s = 8.9 +/- 0.3. The covariance matrix is obtained from 600 lognormal mock catalogues. The 2dFGRS and SDSS constraints agree, and a joint fit reduces the uncertainty to 3 per cent in the distance scale.

We re-fit the infrared spectral energy distributions of 36 Seyfert 2 galaxies using the updated CLUMPY torus models, which include a wider range of cloud number along the equatorial plane, N_0 = 1-15, inner opening angle, and radial distribution index q = 0-3. Compared to earlier fits using the 2006 model grid, the updated models yield smaller torus angular widths with sigma = 30 - 60 degrees, and larger cloud optical depths tau_V = 20-80. The torus radii, determined by the bolometric luminosity, are consistent with 0.1 - 10 pc, a factor of 2 smaller than before. The number of clouds along radial equatorial rays is found to be N_0 ~ 5 - 10. The fitted AGN fraction in the mid-infrared at 12 micron is 60-90 per cent, in agreement with nuclear high-angular resolution data.

Tidal dwarf galaxies can form in the extended tails of interacting galaxies through several mechanisms. In the gravitational instability scenario, gas in the HI-rich tidal tail fragments on scales of 10^8 - 10^9 solar masses, when the Toomre Q parameter drops below unity due to compressive tides and accumulation of material along the tail. Alternatively, collapse can be triggered at the tail tips by the accumulation of stars and gas, where large-scale velocity gradients vanish. Simulations show that the survival of these objects is helped by dark matter in the halo of the progenitor, which provides a deep potential well, and their formation rate depends on the gas fraction of the progenitors and the orbit geometry, with prograde encounters being more efficient.

We propose a scenario in which the Milky Way thick disc formed at z ~ 1.5 - 3 through intense star formation in a gas-rich, turbulent disc. In this clumpy disc picture, gravitational instabilities produce giant star-forming clumps of 10^8 solar masses, which scatter stars, heat the disc vertically and drive inward migration. Star formation rates of 10 - 50 solar masses per year in a gas disc with velocity dispersion of 40 - 60 km/s produce a stellar disc with scale height of 900 pc, much thicker than the present thin disc. The resulting thick disc is alpha-enhanced, with [alpha/Fe] ~ 0.3, because the star formation was rapid, lasting 2-4 Gyr, and ended before type Ia supernovae enriched the gas with iron.

We derive an upper limit on the cosmic string tension from the requirement that radiation from cosmic string loops does not reionize the universe too early. Loops formed by a network of strings emit ionizing photons and heat the gas through wakes, so the optical depth to Thomson scattering produced by string-seeded structure must remain below the measured tau = 0.055 +/- 0.009. For a loop size parameter alpha ~ 0.1 and a reconnection probability p = 1, the models produce early star formation and a damped signature at z > 15. The resulting constraint is G mu < 3 x 10^-7 at 95 per cent confidence, where mu is the string tension and G is Newton's constant, comparable to the limits from the CMB power spectrum.

We assess the accuracy of redshifts derived from HST WFC3/G141 grism spectra for emission-line galaxies at 1.2 < z < 1.9, where Halpha moves through the grism wavelength range and [O III] and Hbeta are detected at the higher redshifts. Using 240 galaxies with ground-based spectroscopic redshifts from Keck/MOSFIRE and VLT/KMOS, we find that the normalised median absolute deviation is sigma_NMAD = 0.003 in (1+z), corresponding to about 1000 km/s, with an outlier fraction of 4 per cent where the grism redshift differs by more than 5 sigma. The dominant failures are due to confusion between [O III] and Halpha and blended lines. The precision improves to 0.002 when two or more lines are detected.

The application of photodissociation region models to the [C II] 158 micron emission of whole galaxies is limited by several effects. The [C II] line arises not only from PDRs but also from ionized gas, the diffuse neutral medium and CO-dark molecular gas, with the ionized medium contributing 10 - 30 per cent of the line. PDR models assume a single plane-parallel slab characterized by gas density and FUV radiation field G_0, whereas galaxies contain a distribution of clouds, which makes the derived values luminosity-weighted averages. The [C II]/FIR ratio saturates at high G_0 as grain charging reduces photoelectric heating efficiency, and optical depth effects at high column density, together with metallicity and variations in carbon abundance, introduce degeneracies in the interpretation.

A reddened star with zero continuum polarization is an interesting case in studies of anomalous extinction sightlines. In the Galaxy, the wavelength of maximum polarization, lambda_max, is correlated with the total-to-selective extinction ratio R_V, so that sightlines with unusual R_V or with large grains typically show strong polarization given the Serkowski law with P_max/E(B-V) < 9 per cent per magnitude. A star with E(B-V) = 1 and R_V = 4 but P < 0.05 per cent implies either that the line of sight passes through a medium with randomly oriented, non-aligned grains, perhaps due to turbulent magnetic field or a field along the line of sight, or that the dust is present in a circumstellar shell or has no alignment mechanism.

We quantify how the number of detected photometric bands affects the photometric redshift uncertainties of ALMA-identified submillimetre galaxies. For 150 sources with spectroscopic redshifts, we run template fitting with sub-sets of the available UV to near-infrared bands, from 3 to 20 filters. Sources with fewer than 7 detections have a normalised median absolute deviation of sigma_NMAD = 0.12 and 30 per cent catastrophic outliers, while those with 12 or more bands reach sigma_NMAD = 0.04 and 8 per cent outliers. The 68 per cent confidence interval of p(z) narrows from delta z = 1.0 to 0.3. Detection in the K band and IRAC channels is crucial because many sources are faint at optical wavelengths due to heavy dust obscuration, and a Balmer break is not well sampled otherwise.

The intergalactic medium attenuates Lyman-alpha photons, particularly on the blue side of the line, with increasing efficiency toward higher redshift. At z < 4, the IGM transmission blueward of line centre is of order 70 - 90 per cent, but it falls to 30 - 50 per cent at z ~ 6 and less than 10 per cent at z > 7 where the neutral hydrogen fraction rises. The double-peaked profiles that emerge from the interstellar medium therefore appear as single red peaks, with the blue peak suppressed and the red peak shifted by 100 - 300 km/s. Damping-wing absorption from neutral gas near the source further reduces the flux, so the fraction of double-peaked emitters decreases from 30 per cent at z = 3 to nearly zero at z > 6.

Ultra-hard X-ray surveys such as the Swift/BAT survey, covering the 14 - 195 keV band, are nearly unbiased in the detection of obscured AGN, because photons above 10 keV are able to penetrate columns up to N_H ~ 10^24 cm^-2 with limited attenuation. Only in the Compton-thick regime, N_H > 1.5 x 10^24 cm^-2, does Compton scattering reduce the observed flux significantly. The 105-month BAT catalogue reaches a flux limit of 8 x 10^-12 erg/cm^2/s over 90 per cent of the sky, and 4 x 10^-12 erg/cm^2/s in the deepest regions, detecting about 1,600 sources. About 70 per cent of the AGN are classified as Seyfert 2 or have absorbed X-ray spectra with N_H > 10^22 cm^-2, and the selection is independent of host galaxy properties.

We study the origin of bright UV clumps in simulated galaxies at z > 5 using a cosmological zoom-in suite with a resolution of 10 pc. We trace the stars of each clump back to their formation sites and find that 20 - 30 per cent of the clumps are accreted satellites, while most, 70 - 80 per cent, form in situ through fragmentation of the turbulent, gas-rich disc. Ex-situ clumps tend to have higher stellar masses, 10^8 - 10^9 solar masses, higher metallicity offsets and older stellar ages, and are found at larger galactocentric radii, while in-situ clumps are more compact, younger (less than 50 Myr), and more numerous. The clump fraction in UV luminosity reaches 30 - 50 per cent, and the clump masses are consistent with the Toomre instability scale.

We examine the star formation cycles in the nuclear regions of simulated galaxies using high-resolution hydrodynamic simulations with explicit stellar feedback. We find a transition at a young stellar surface density of Sigma_* ~ 10^3 solar masses per pc^2 that separates two regimes. Below this threshold, feedback from radiation pressure and supernovae is insufficient to halt gas infall, and the gas collapses on a free-fall time, leading to rapid star formation. Above the threshold, the momentum injected by feedback exceeds the gravitational pull and drives blowout cycles, expelling the gas at velocities of several hundred km/s, with a period of about 5-10 Myr. The threshold depends weakly on the gas fraction and scales approximately with the stellar surface density where the Eddington flux balances gravity.

We present a reverberation mapping campaign of Fe II emission in a sample of 25 AGN with long-term optical monitoring. The Fe II lags relative to the continuum, measured by cross-correlation of light curves in the 4434 - 4684 Angstrom range, are systematically longer than the Hbeta lags measured for the same objects. For the sample, the ratio tau(Fe II)/tau(Hbeta) has a mean value of 1.9 +/- 0.4, with lags of 20 - 60 days in the rest frame for sources with L_5100 ~ 10^44 erg/s. This suggests that the Fe II-emitting gas lies at larger radii than the Hbeta region, probably at the outer edge of the broad-line region or near the dust sublimation radius, with a lower velocity dispersion, consistent with its narrower line profile.

The Hubble eXtreme Deep Field (XDF) is the deepest image of the sky obtained with HST, assembled from 2003 - 2012 observations with ACS and WFC3 in 9 bands, from F435W to F160W, covering 4.7 square arcminutes to 5-sigma depth of 29.8 AB. More recent JWST imaging includes NIRCam observations from the JADES programme in F090W, F115W, F150W, F200W, F277W, F356W, F410M, and F444W, with 5-sigma depths of 30 - 31 AB, and MIRI imaging with the F560W filter to 28.6 AB over a smaller 2.4 square arcminute region from the MIDIS programme, enabling rest-frame near-infrared coverage at z = 6 - 10. All data were reduced onto a common pixel grid of 0.03 arcsec.

We study the dependence of X-ray absorption and Eddington ratio on C IV emission-line properties in a sample of broad absorption line quasars with Chandra and XMM-Newton data. The X-ray weakness, quantified by the optical-to-X-ray spectral slope offset delta alpha_ox, increases with the C IV blueshift and decreasing rest-frame equivalent width. The absorbing column density derived from hardness ratios has N_H ~ 10^22 - 10^24 cm^-2 and is larger in quasars with C IV blueshifts above 3000 km/s, where the equivalent width is smaller than 20 Angstroms. The Eddington ratio estimated from Hbeta shows that these systems accrete at L/L_Edd > 0.5, and the strong shielding gas is consistent with a radiation-driven wind scenario.

We perform one-dimensional and three-dimensional radiation hydrodynamic simulations of the envelope of an isolated massive star of 50 solar masses near the Eddington limit. The iron opacity bump at T ~ 1.8 x 10^5 K produces a density inversion and a convective zone, with turbulent velocities of 10 - 20 km/s. We find that the envelope shows a time-variable, clumpy structure but that this does not generate a persistent outflow in the form of a steady wind, and only a small fraction, below 10^-6 solar masses per year, of the material becomes unbound. Mass loss is episodic and occurs when the radiation force exceeds gravity locally, and the average mass-loss rate is lower than that required by observations, which implies that additional processes, such as pulsations or binary interaction, are necessary.

We compare the growth of black holes in cluster-mass haloes of 10^14-10^15 solar masses from z = 6 to z = 0 in semi-analytic models and cosmological hydrodynamic simulations. Both approaches predict that the progenitors of cluster central galaxies host black holes of 10^8 - 10^9 solar masses by z = 6, but they differ in the growth history. In semi-analytic models the black hole mass grows predominantly through merger-driven accretion in the quasar mode at z > 2, followed by a radio mode, with mergers contributing 20 - 40 per cent of the final mass. In simulations, gas accretion dominates and mass growth from mergers is less than 10 per cent. The final black hole masses differ by 0.3 - 0.5 dex, with the simulations giving a flatter dependence on halo mass.

We show that a delayed first-order phase transition during reheating can seed density perturbations. If the transition completes in different regions at slightly different times, the local expansion history, and hence the energy density at a fixed time, varies from patch to patch. The bubbles nucleate at a rate Gamma(t) ~ exp(beta t), and the resulting delay in the end of reheating, delta t, has a distribution with variance of order sigma^2 ~ 1/beta^2, so that the curvature perturbation is zeta ~ H delta t ~ H/beta. For the power spectrum amplitude P_zeta = 2.1 x 10^-9 we require beta/H ~ 2 x 10^4. We estimate the variance with the first-passage-time approach, with the delta-N formalism relating the perturbation to the fluctuation of the number of e-folds.

We test whether fitting JWST photometry with spectral templates designed for very high redshift galaxies can lower the inferred stellar masses of the early massive candidates. Standard SED fitting with templates of solar metallicity, a Chabrier initial mass function and a delayed star formation history yields stellar masses of 10^10 - 10^11 solar masses at z = 7 - 10, in tension with the halo mass function in LCDM. When using a template set with young bursty star formation, low metallicity (0.1 solar), high ionization parameters, and strong nebular continuum and emission lines, the stellar masses decrease by 0.3 - 0.6 dex, with an average reduction of a factor of three. This alleviates much of the tension, bringing the maximum stellar mass density to within the 2 sigma bounds, though the most extreme sources remain difficult to reconcile.

Binaries formed by gas-assisted capture are not always stable. We find that a captured pair becomes unbound if its separation exceeds a fraction of the Hill radius, r_H = a (m/3M)^(1/3), above which tidal forces from the background dominate and the binary is disrupted. Capture in the gravitationally focused regime, where the relative velocity at infinity is smaller than the escape velocity at the encounter pericentre, is efficient when the dissipation by gas dynamical friction removes the orbital energy in a single passage. For a gas density of 10^-10 g/cm^3 and a relative velocity of 10 km/s, the resulting binaries with separations below 0.1 r_H are stable against tidal disruption, while wider ones are soon destroyed in encounters with other members of the cluster.

Posterior predictive checks are a Bayesian tool for assessing whether a fitted model is an adequate description of the data. After obtaining the posterior distribution of the model parameters, one draws parameter values from the posterior, simulates replicate datasets, and compares a test statistic computed from the replicates with the value from the observed data. In X-ray spectral fitting with Poisson counts, one can use the Cash statistic or likelihood as test statistic, since chi-squared is not valid in the low-count regime, and calculate a posterior predictive p-value, the fraction of simulated datasets with a statistic exceeding the observed one. Values near 0 or 1 indicate model misfit, while values near 0.5 indicate consistent data, and residual structure can be visualised by plotting the data against the predictive band.

The most massive and luminous galaxies at z = 7 - 9 require a high integrated star formation efficiency, epsilon = M_*/(f_b M_halo), of 0.3 - 0.6 when matched against the abundance of dark matter haloes in LCDM, which is a factor of 3-10 above the value of 0.1 - 0.2 found at lower redshift. The efficiency is particularly high for objects with UV magnitudes brighter than M_UV = -21. A top-heavy initial mass function, with a high-mass slope of -2.0 or a characteristic mass of 1 solar mass, increases the UV luminosity per unit stellar mass by a factor of 3 - 4, allowing a lower efficiency of epsilon ~ 0.1 - 0.2 to explain the observed UV luminosity function, though stellar masses are lower and metal enrichment is changed.

Optical and near-infrared P-Cygni profiles have been detected in only a few X-ray binaries, indicating the presence of cool, dense outflows. In the black hole candidate V404 Cygni during its 2015 outburst, H-alpha and He I 10830 showed blueshifted absorption troughs at velocities of 1000 - 2000 km/s. In the neutron star systems such as Sco X-1 and in the black hole binary GRS 1915+105, He I 10830 P-Cygni absorption was seen at -1000 km/s during the hard states. In the ultracompact binary 4U 1820-30 the profiles were observed at 500 km/s. Mass-loss rates inferred from these profiles are 10^-8 - 10^-7 solar masses per year, and the outflow is probably a thermal or radiation-driven wind from the outer accretion disc, with the profiles appearing at a high inclination.

We estimate the Eddington ratio of super-early galaxies such as JADES-GS-z14-0, at z = 14.3, to assess whether radiation-driven outflows can clear dust and gas. With a stellar mass of 10^8.7 solar masses, a UV luminosity of 10^45.7 erg/s and an effective radius of 260 pc, the bolometric luminosity-to-mass ratio corresponds to an Eddington ratio of Gamma ~ 0.05 - 0.1 when computed using only electron scattering opacity.
