Taking into account the dust opacity, which boosts the effective Eddington ratio by the factor kappa_d/kappa_es ~ 100 - 1000 for dust-to-gas ratios of 0.1 times the Milky Way value, one gets Gamma_eff ~ 1 - 10, so that the dust-boosted radiation pressure exceeds gravity and can drive strong outflows, thereby explaining the blue UV slopes.

Stacking the NIRSpec G395M spectra of 18 little red dots at 5 < z < 7 reveals a number of rest-frame near-infrared absorption features. We detect the Ca II triplet at 8498, 8542 and 8662 Angstroms in absorption in a subset of the sample, with a combined equivalent width of 2 - 4 Angstroms, a significance of 4 sigma, and a velocity offset of -100 to -200 km/s relative to the narrow lines. We also see a weaker Na I D absorption, and Ca II triplet emission is not significantly detected. Such absorption would imply a low-temperature, dense gas component rather than a stellar origin, as an old stellar population would exhibit stronger photospheric lines and a CO bandhead.

The characteristic V-shaped continuum of little red dots, with a blue rest-frame UV slope (beta ~ -2) and a red optical slope (beta_opt > 0), with a turnover near the Balmer limit at 3646-4000 Angstroms, has been interpreted in several ways. In a first scenario, the UV and optical light arise from distinct components, with a reddened AGN dominating the optical and a faint, unobscured star-forming host or scattered AGN light producing the UV. In a second, a Balmer break from either an evolved stellar population or dense gas absorption around the black hole produces the turnover. In a third, the AGN continuum is itself intrinsically curved, since a thick envelope with a temperature of 5000 K shapes a blackbody-like spectrum and dust is not required.

V-shaped spectral energy distributions are not exclusive to little red dots. A fraction of 5-10 per cent of the high-redshift compact galaxies in JWST surveys that satisfy no little red dot colour selection also show a turnover near 3600 - 4000 Angstroms with a blue UV and a rising optical continuum, including post-starburst and dusty star-forming galaxies with an unobscured UV component. Local analogues such as dust-reddened type 1 quasars and Seyfert 2 galaxies with scattered light display similar shapes. However, the little red dots are distinguished by the sharpness of the inflection, the lack of hot dust emission in MIRI and the compactness of the sources below 100 pc, which makes the combination of properties, as opposed to the V-shape alone, unusual.

A small number of little red dots have been observed in great detail with deep spectroscopy and multiwavelength follow-up. These include A2744-QSO1 at z = 7.04, a triply lensed source behind Abell 2744 with a Balmer break, broad Hbeta and a dynamical black hole mass measurement, and The Cliff (RUBIES-UDS-154183) at z = 3.55, with a very strong Balmer break and Balmer absorption features. Other well-studied examples include UNCOVER-45924, the brightest known little red dot at z = 4.47, RUBIES-BLAGN-1 at z = 3.1, and the local analogues J1025+1402 at z = 0.1 and other lower-redshift analogues in SDSS. These sources have high signal-to-noise NIRSpec G395H, MIRI and ALMA data.

The dense nuclear stellar cluster hypothesis proposes that the red optical continua and Balmer breaks of little red dots are produced by compact clusters of evolved stars, without any black hole contribution to the continuum. In this picture, a stellar mass of 10^9 - 10^10 solar masses is packed within an effective radius of order 10 - 50 pc, giving stellar densities above 10^8 solar masses per cubic parsec. The Balmer break arises from A-type and later stars with ages of 100 - 500 Myr, and the broad lines come from a combination of high-velocity dispersion, sigma > 500 km/s, and stellar collisions, or from a low-mass AGN. The model naturally explains the compact sizes, but faces difficulties with the lack of stellar absorption lines and the required stellar densities exceeding the Eddington limit for dynamical collapse.

The far-infrared fine-structure lines provide a dust-insensitive probe of the interstellar medium in the host. We detect [O III] 88 um and [C II] 158 um at S/N of 5 and 4, respectively, with a line ratio L[O III]/L[C II] of roughly 3, typical of compact, highly ionized star-forming systems. Comparing the [O III]/[C II] and [N II] ratios with photoionization models computed with Cloudy over a grid of ionization parameter and density, we infer a gas-phase metallicity of Z ~ 0.3-0.5 Zsun, consistent with the sub-solar value of 12+log(O/H) ~ 8.3 from rest-optical lines. Solar metallicity is disfavoured at about 2 sigma, and the dynamical mass of the host is of order 10^10 Msun.

For Case B recombination at an electron temperature of 10^4 K and in the low-density limit (n_e ~ 10^2 cm^-3), the intrinsic Balmer decrement is H-alpha/H-beta = 2.86, with H-gamma/H-beta = 0.47 and H-delta/H-beta = 0.26. Lyman-alpha is produced at a much higher rate, since roughly 0.68 of recombinations yield a Ly-alpha photon, giving Ly-alpha/H-beta ~ 23 and Ly-alpha/H-alpha ~ 8.1 in the absence of dust and resonant-scattering losses. The ratios depend only weakly on temperature, with H-alpha/H-beta rising to 2.74 at 2x10^4 K and 3.04 at 5x10^3 K. Observed Ly-alpha/H-beta values well below ~23 therefore indicate absorption by dust or escape of Ly-alpha photons outside the aperture.

Candidates were drawn from the WISE all-sky catalogue in the SDSS Stripe 82 region by requiring a 22 um detection with flux density S22 > 3 mJy, together with a red mid-infrared colour W1-W2 > 0.8 and an extremely high ratio of mid-infrared to optical flux, with R-band magnitudes fainter than 23 in the deep co-added imaging. Obscured type 2 quasars are expected to be faint in the optical but luminous at rest-frame 6-12 um, where hot dust re-radiates the nuclear emission. We obtained follow-up spectroscopy of 48 candidates with Keck/LRIS and Gemini/GMOS. About 70 percent showed narrow high-ionization lines such as C IV and [Ne V] without broad components at z = 1.5-2.5, confirming them as luminous type 2 quasars with L_bol > 10^46 erg/s.

Stellar masses and star formation rates were derived assuming a Chabrier initial mass function, a log-normal form below 1 Msun joined to a Salpeter power-law slope of -2.35 at higher masses, integrated from 0.1 to 100 Msun. Compared with a pure Salpeter IMF over the same mass range, this choice lowers stellar masses and star formation rates by a factor of about 1.7 (0.24 dex), because fewer low-mass stars contribute to the mass-to-light ratio. Where literature values were quoted for a Kroupa or Salpeter IMF, we rescaled them to the Chabrier IMF using the corresponding conversion factors of 1.06 and 0.61 respectively, so that all quantities are directly comparable.

To estimate intrinsic hard X-ray luminosities we adopt a luminosity-dependent bolometric correction, k_X = L_bol/L_2-10keV, which increases with luminosity as the X-ray emission becomes weaker relative to the optical/UV disc. The adopted calibration yields k_X ~ 10-15 at L_bol ~ 10^43-10^44 erg/s, rising to ~ 20 at L_bol = 10^45 erg/s and to k_X ~ 70-100 at L_bol ~ 10^47 erg/s. The relation is built from template spectral energy distributions of type 1 AGN spanning 10^41-10^47 erg/s, and the intrinsic scatter is about 0.3-0.4 dex. The correlation between k_X and Eddington ratio is also consistent with this trend, with k_X exceeding 50 for lambda_Edd > 0.1.

We measure C III] 1909 in stacked VANDELS spectra of star-forming galaxies at 3 < z < 4, a regime where Ly-alpha is shifted into the optical but is strongly modulated by resonant scattering and the geometry of neutral hydrogen. The C III] rest-frame equivalent width is detected in individual spectra for roughly 15 percent of the sample, with a median EW of 2-3 A and a tail extending beyond 10 A for the lowest-mass, bluest galaxies. Because C III] is a collisionally excited, non-resonant doublet, it traces the ionizing radiation field and the metallicity without the escape-fraction uncertainties of Ly-alpha. Using C III] as a redshift indicator reduces systemic velocity offsets from ~ 400 km/s for Ly-alpha to below 100 km/s.

Absorption from the metastable n=2 level of hydrogen, seen as Balmer lines H-alpha through H-delta and Ca II H&K, is detected in a small subset of FeLoBAL quasars. Using the apparent optical depth method and assuming partial covering, we derive H(n=2) column densities of N ~ 10^14-10^15 cm^-2, from which a total hydrogen column of order 10^22-10^23 cm^-2 is inferred in the ionization-bounded slab behind the front. The absorption troughs are blueshifted by 3000-6000 km/s with widths of ~ 1000 km/s, and the outflow velocities of Balmer, Fe II and Mg II absorption are consistent within the errors. The high population of the n=2 level implies electron densities of n_e > 10^6 cm^-3, placing the absorber at a distance of ~ 1-10 pc.

Several of the broad-line AGN at z = 4-7 show narrow, deep absorption features superposed on the broad H-alpha, H-beta and He I 10830 emission, blueshifted by only 100-300 km/s relative to the narrow-line redshift. The absorption in H-alpha reaches depths of 30-60 percent of the local continuum, indicating a high covering fraction. Because absorption in Balmer lines requires a substantial population of n=2 hydrogen, the gas must be dense (n_H > 10^9 cm^-3) and shielded from the ionizing continuum, while the presence of He I absorption from the 2^3S metastable level independently supports this picture. The inferred column densities, N(H n=2) ~ 10^15-10^16 cm^-2, are comparable to those in Balmer-absorption quasars in the local universe.

We examine whether nuclear star clusters (NSCs) and central supermassive black holes can share common scaling relations with the host's properties. A stability analysis of the coevolving system shows that an NSC of mass M_NSC ~ 10^7 Msun is dynamically stable against runaway growth of a central black hole as long as the black hole mass remains below ~ 0.1 M_NSC. At larger masses the black hole dominates the potential within its radius of influence, the two-body relaxation time lengthens, and the cluster is gradually depleted by tidal disruption and loss-cone refilling. The resulting M_NSC-M_BH relation transitions from NSC-dominated in low-mass spheroids to black-hole-dominated in massive ellipticals, which naturally explains the observed M_NSC ~ sigma^2.1 scaling and its steepening at M_* ~ 10^11 Msun.

Triaxial dark matter halos support a population of centrophilic orbits, notably box orbits and chaotic orbits, which pass arbitrarily close to the centre and are responsible for the triaxial shape. We construct N-body halos with axis ratios b/a ~ 0.8 and c/a ~ 0.6 and grow a central baryonic condensation adiabatically, with the mass reaching 1-3 percent of the halo mass. A growing central concentration scatters box orbits chaotically, as their repeated close passages deflect them, and the fraction of chaotic orbits rises from ~ 10 percent to above 50 percent inside 0.1 r_vir. The Lyapunov exponents increase with the central mass, and the halo rapidly becomes more spherical, with c/a rising to above 0.85 within a few dynamical times.

Posterior distributions were sampled with emcee, a pure-Python implementation of the affine-invariant ensemble sampler of Goodman and Weare. The sampler evolves an ensemble of walkers whose proposal moves are built from the positions of the other walkers, which makes it invariant under affine transformations of the parameter space and hence well suited to anisotropic, correlated posteriors with essentially one tuning parameter, the stretch scale a = 2. We used 64 walkers and ran each chain for 20000 steps after a burn-in of 5000 steps, which exceeds 50 times the integrated autocorrelation time estimated for every parameter. Convergence was checked by inspecting trace plots, and the acceptance fraction was 0.3.

In the standard geometrically thin, optically thick accretion disc model, gas follows nearly circular Keplerian orbits and angular momentum is transported outwards by a turbulent viscosity parameterized by alpha. Each annulus radiates locally as a blackbody, giving an effective temperature T(r) proportional to r^(-3/4) and a multi-colour spectrum that peaks in the UV for supermassive black holes. Energy dissipated in the disc is gravitational binding energy released down to the innermost stable circular orbit, so the radiative efficiency, eta = L/(Mdot c^2), is 0.057 for a non-rotating Schwarzschild black hole and increases to 0.42 for a maximally spinning Kerr black hole with prograde orbits. A canonical value of eta = 0.1 is typically adopted.

We stack the Chandra 2-7 Ms images at the positions of 300 photometrically selected little red dots, excluding those with individually detected X-ray counterparts. No signal is detected in the soft (0.5-2 keV) or hard (2-8 keV) band, and the 3 sigma upper limit on the mean rest-frame 2-10 keV luminosity is L_X < 3x10^42 erg/s. Adopting the bolometric luminosities inferred from the broad Halpha lines, this corresponds to an X-ray to bolometric ratio at least one order of magnitude below the value expected for typical AGN with the same luminosity. Even for a Compton-thin column of N_H ~ 10^23 cm^-2, the stacked limit remains in tension with a standard AGN-dominated spectral energy distribution unless the X-ray emission is intrinsically weak or the sources are Compton-thick.

Total fluxes were measured in elliptical Kron apertures, following the adaptive-aperture scheme introduced for faint galaxy photometry. The first-moment radius r_1 = sum(r I(r))/sum(I(r)) is computed from the pixel intensities within an isophotal detection region, and the aperture is defined as an ellipse, with the shape given by the second moments of the light distribution, of semi-major axis equal to k r_1 with k = 2.5. For a galaxy with exponential or de Vaucouleurs profile, such an aperture encloses roughly 90 percent of the total flux, essentially independent of the apparent magnitude or the seeing. The remaining flux outside the aperture is corrected assuming a Sersic profile, and typically amounts to 0.1 mag for faint sources.

The H-alpha line flux can be isolated from broad-band and narrow-band images through a three-filter method in which two continuum bands bracket the line. The continuum underneath the narrow-band filter is estimated by linear interpolation between a blue broad-band (for instance r) and a red broad-band (for instance i) filter, after the line contribution to the broad band centred on H-alpha is subtracted. Concretely, the line flux is F_line = Delta_NB (f_NB - f_cont), where f_cont is the interpolated continuum flux density and Delta_NB is the effective width of the narrow-band filter. Corrections are applied for [N II] contamination, typically 0.3 of the blended flux, and for the filter transmission profile at the redshift of the source.

MIRI imaging at 7.7-21 um reveals a source at z = 6.6 whose rest-frame near-infrared emission shows a clear excess over the stellar continuum predicted from the NIRCam photometry. The mid-infrared SED rises steeply at rest-frame 1-3 um, with F_21/F_7.7 > 3, a signature of hot dust at 800-1200 K heated by an obscured AGN. The galaxy is otherwise a typical star-forming system with M_* ~ 10^9.5 Msun, SFR ~ 30 Msun/yr and narrow [O III] and H-alpha lines, without a broad component down to a flux limit of 10^-18 erg/s/cm^2. The AGN contribution to the rest-frame 3 um luminosity is about 50 percent, implying a bolometric luminosity of ~ 10^45 erg/s hidden behind column densities N_H > 10^23 cm^-2.

We generate mock observations from the hydrodynamical simulation snapshots using the publicly available radiative transfer package SKIRT, which performs Monte Carlo transfer of photon packets through the dust distribution while taking the stellar populations and AGN as sources. The star particles are assigned spectral energy distributions from stellar population synthesis templates according to age and metallicity, while the dust is traced by the metal content of the cold gas with a dust-to-metal ratio of 0.3. The output consists of integral-field data cubes, broad-band images convolved with the PSF of the relevant instrument, and noise appropriate for a given exposure time, so that the observables can be analysed with the same tools as real data, including the photometry and Sersic fits.

We evaluate the accreted black hole mass density at z ~ 6 implied by the UV-selected quasar luminosity function using a Soltan-type argument. Integrating the luminosity function down to M_1450 = -22 and adopting a bolometric correction of 4.4 and a radiative efficiency of 0.1, the accumulated mass density is rho_BH ~ 10^2.5 Msun/Mpc^3. This represents only about 1 percent of the total local black hole mass density of 4x10^5 Msun/Mpc^3, and even less than the total mass density expected to be assembled by z = 6 if the growth proceeds at the Eddington limit. The majority of the black hole mass at z ~ 6 must thus reside in fainter or obscured AGN, including those missed by UV selection, with the luminous quasars accounting for no more than a few percent.

The bulge-to-total light ratio decreases systematically along the Hubble sequence. In the I band, the mean B/T is 0.6-0.7 for S0 galaxies, 0.4-0.5 for Sa, 0.3 for Sb, 0.2 for Sc, and below 0.1 for Sd-Sm systems, with a scatter of 0.1-0.15 at fixed type. The values depend strongly on the passband, as the bulge is redder than the disc: B/T in the B band is typically 30-50 percent lower than in the K band, where Sb galaxies have B/T ~ 0.35. Decompositions with a Sersic bulge of free index and an exponential disc give B/T that are about 0.05 higher than fixed de Vaucouleurs bulges, which reflects that the pseudobulges in later types have n ~ 1-2.

We compare the photometric properties of galaxies in the FLARES zoom simulations with HST-based observations at z = 5-10. After applying a dust attenuation model in which the optical depth scales with the line-of-sight metal column density, the predicted rest-frame UV luminosity functions are in good agreement with the observed Schechter functions at M_UV < -19, within 0.2 dex across z = 5-8, and the bright-end over-density is captured by sampling regions of extreme over-density. The simulated UV continuum slopes, beta ~ -2.2 at M_UV = -20 and steepening to -2.6 at the faint end, are consistent with the observations. At z > 8 the simulation slightly underestimates the abundance of the brightest galaxies by a factor of ~ 2-3.

Using the SDSS spectroscopic sample, we measure the size-luminosity and size-mass relations for local early- and late-type galaxies separated by Sersic index (n = 2.5) and colour. Late-type galaxies follow R_50 proportional to L^0.2-0.3 at fixed luminosity, with a mean half-light radius of about 3.5 kpc at M_r = -20.5, with a scatter of 0.3 dex. Early-type galaxies show a steeper relation, R_50 proportional to L^0.6, with larger sizes at the bright end and a turn-over at M_r ~ -20.5 where the relation steepens. In stellar mass, the relation for late-types is R proportional to M_*^0.14 below the pivot mass and M_*^0.39 above it, while early-types follow R proportional to M_*^0.56 with a scatter of 0.15 dex.

The Cliff is a little red dot at z = 3.55 with a remarkably sharp Balmer break and a V-shaped continuum. We fit the NIRSpec prism spectrum with stellar population models, assuming a Small Magellanic Cloud dust law, and find a stellar mass of log(M_*/Msun) = 10.0-10.5 and V-band attenuation A_V ~ 0.5-1 mag. Such a stellar mass in a compact region of effective radius ~ 100 pc would imply an implausibly high stellar mass surface density, exceeding 10^10 Msun/kpc^2. The best-fit star formation history requires a recent burst of a few tens of Myr, and the stellar-only model provides a poor fit to the Balmer break depth, leaving residuals that are better explained by dense gas absorption.

Mergers of dark matter halos can heat the gas in atomic cooling halos by shocks and by adiabatic compression of the gas during the merger, raising the virial temperature and suppressing H2 formation. In simulations without a Lyman-Werner radiation background, we find that in about 10 percent of halos the gas temperature stays above 8000 K for a few tens of Myr following a major merger with mass ratio > 1:3, which allows direct collapse. Gas then collapses isothermally at about 8000 K with accretion rates of 0.1-1 Msun/yr, leading to seeds of 10^4-10^5 Msun. The seed mass distribution is correlated with the merger history, with more massive seeds forming in halos with recent mergers and higher spin.

We fit the joint spectro-photometric SED, including NIRSpec prism spectra and NIRCam and MIRI photometry, using a model with a broad-line AGN component and a stellar population component. Host stellar masses are derived after subtracting the AGN contribution to the rest-frame optical continuum, yielding M_* ~ 10^8.5-10^10 Msun for AGN at 3 < z < 7. The resulting black hole to stellar mass ratio is M_BH/M_* ~ 0.03-0.1 on average, offset by 1-2 dex above the local relation of ~ 0.001 and by ~ 0.8 dex relative to local active samples. The ratio shows mild positive evolution with redshift, M_BH/M_* proportional to (1+z)^1.5. Accounting for selection effects, which bias the sample towards overmassive black holes, reduces but does not eliminate the offset.

Dust emission is modelled with the Draine & Li prescription, in which the grain population is a mixture of amorphous silicate, graphite and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) particles with a size distribution that reproduces the Milky Way extinction curve. The bulk of the dust, with a fraction 1-gamma, is heated by a uniform radiation field U_min, while a fraction gamma is exposed to a power-law distribution of starlight intensities, dM/dU proportional to U^-alpha with U between U_min and U_max = 10^6 and alpha = 2. The free parameters are the PAH mass fraction q_PAH, U_min, gamma and the total dust mass. For our galaxies we find q_PAH ~ 2-4 percent, U_min ~ 5-15, and gamma ~ 0.02, with dust masses 10^7-10^8 Msun.

We cross-matched the XMM-COSMOS point sources with the Chandra COSMOS Legacy Survey, whose 0.5 arcsec positional accuracy considerably improves on the XMM uncertainty of about 2 arcsec. Chandra positions confirmed the optical counterpart originally assigned using the likelihood-ratio method for about 90 percent of the sources, while the counterpart changed for 7 percent, mostly cases with ambiguous multiple candidates within the XMM error circle, and the remaining 3 percent had no Chandra counterpart or were resolved into two X-ray sources. The reliability of the likelihood-ratio matching was a function of the optical magnitude, and changes occurred predominantly for faint counterparts with i_AB > 24 and for X-ray fluxes below 10^-14 erg/s/cm^2 in the 0.5-2 keV band.

Adding a point-spread-function-convolved point source at the centre of a galaxy that also has a bulge profile introduces strong degeneracies between the two components. If the Sersic index of the bulge is left free, the fit tends to give a high index n > 4 with large effective radius to compensate for an under-fitted nucleus, or the point source absorbs flux from a cuspy bulge, with the AGN fraction biased by up to 0.3 dex. Errors in the PSF model, such as mismatch in the core width by 10 percent, leave residuals in the central pixels that propagate into the host photometry, and the problem worsens at low S/N or with a point source contributing less than 10 percent of the total light. Fixing the Sersic index and masking the core helps a little.

When two black holes merge, the remnant has a mass lower than that of the initial binary by a few percent, as gravitational waves carry away energy, and the loss occurs on a time scale of order the binary orbital period, far shorter than the orbital time of the surrounding disc gas. Disc gas at radius r orbiting the original binary mass M then finds itself in a potential with a mass lower by approximately 5 percent, and its orbits become slightly eccentric. The sudden change in the gravitational potential launches an outward-propagating spiral density wave, a ripple, in the circumbinary disc. In hydrodynamical simulations the wave steepens into a shock, with a luminosity increase by a factor of about 2 on the viscous time scale, a potential electromagnetic precursor or afterglow.

The gamma-ray-emitting narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxy shows markedly different variability across the radio band. At high frequencies (37 GHz), the flux density varies by a factor of 3 over a few months, with a fractional variability amplitude F_var = 0.6, and the brightness temperature exceeds 10^12 K, requiring Doppler boosting with delta ~ 5-10. At low frequencies (1.4 GHz) the flux density is almost constant to within 10 percent over a decade. The radio spectrum is flat to inverted above 5 GHz, and steepens below. Flares progress from high to low frequencies, with a delay of weeks to months, as the shocked region becomes optically thin, which is the standard behaviour of a relativistic jet in blazars.

From the SDSS DR7 quasar catalogue we selected objects at 0.1 < z < 0.7 with broad H-beta and median S/N > 20 per pixel over 4000-5500 A, in order to constrain the Fe II template fitting. We excluded spectra with broad absorption lines, with strong host-galaxy contamination (identified by Ca H&K breaks or stellar absorption features) and with bad pixels or sky-subtraction problems in the fitting windows. The Galactic extinction correction used the Schlegel map, and the spectra were shifted to the rest frame via the redshift of [O III] 5007. After the cleaning procedure about 4,000 of the original 9,000 spectra remained. The pseudo-continuum was modelled with a power law and an Fe II template convolved with a Gaussian broadened to the width of the Balmer lines.

The waveform model is a phenomenological frequency-domain description of the inspiral, merger and ringdown of black hole binaries with spins aligned with the orbital angular momentum. The amplitude and phase are calibrated by hybrid waveforms constructed by matching post-Newtonian or effective-one-body inspirals to numerical relativity simulations. We assess the accuracy by computing the mismatch (one minus the maximised overlap) between the model and 100 numerical relativity hybrids, spanning mass ratios q = 1-18 and dimensionless spins chi = -0.85 to 0.85, using the Advanced LIGO design noise curve for total masses of 10-300 Msun. The mismatch is below 1 percent for most of the parameter space, and below 3 percent in all cases, with the largest errors for high mass ratios and large anti-aligned spins.

To test whether the Herschel-observed sample is representative, we compare its distributions in redshift and luminosity to the parent SDSS DR7 quasar sample in the same range of z = 2-3.5. The Herschel targets, selected from the fields of the HerMES and H-ATLAS surveys, span the bolometric luminosity range 10^46-10^47.5 erg/s, and a two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test finds no significant difference, with a p-value of 0.4 in redshift and 0.2 in i-band absolute magnitude M_i. The median luminosity differs by 0.1 dex, comparable to the sampling error. The area covered, however, is small and cosmic variance may matter, but there is no indication of a bias towards unusually far-infrared luminous or optically bright quasars, so the sample is representative of the SDSS type-1 population.

In compact massive starbursts at z ~ 2, the star formation rates inferred from the total infrared luminosity are higher than the radio-based values by a factor of 3-5 on average. Using the FIR-radio correlation calibrated in local star-forming galaxies, with q_IR = 2.6, the radio luminosity at 1.4 GHz predicts a SFR of ~ 100 Msun/yr compared with an IR-based SFR of ~ 400 Msun/yr. This suggests either suppressed radio emission, due to free-free absorption in dense gas or to the cooling of cosmic-ray electrons through inverse-Compton scattering off the intense photon field, or a contribution to the infrared luminosity from heating by an obscured AGN or an older stellar population. The offset increases with surface density of star formation.

The amplitude of the optical power spectral density (PSD) at a fixed variability frequency of 1/(100 d) anticorrelates with the AGN bolometric luminosity, scaling as L_bol^-0.5, consistent with the variability amplitude being lower for more massive systems. At fixed luminosity, the amplitude is further anticorrelated with the Eddington ratio, with a slope of about -0.3, suggesting that the amplitude is controlled by black hole mass. The PSD slope is steeper than -2 at high frequencies, with a mean of -2.5. Outliers, such as AGN showing flares, or those with large photometric errors, flatten the fitted slopes, and low-amplitude objects in noisy light curves bias the amplitude estimates high by 0.2 dex; we correct for this with simulated light curves and robust fitting with 3 sigma clipping.

In dynamical capture channels for Population III remnants in dense clusters, the formation of binary black holes inevitably leads to systems with more than two black holes. Triple and quadruple systems form through three-body binary-single encounters, and we treat the interaction explicitly using a few-body scattering code, tracking each encounter until the system is either disrupted or ends as a stable hierarchical configuration. We find that multiple systems comprise about 20-30 percent of dynamically assembled merging systems, with a significant fraction of the mergers occurring in hierarchical triples via the Kozai-Lidov mechanism. Mergers in higher-order systems enhance the overall merger rate by 10-40 percent, with an estimated total Pop III BBH merger rate of ~ 0.1-10 per Gpc^3 per yr at z ~ 10.

We compare the rotation and dispersion measure profiles in the circumgalactic medium (CGM) of simulated Milky Way-mass galaxies with observational constraints from fast radio bursts and background radio sources. The simulated galaxies have halo gas with temperatures of 10^6 K and a mean DM contribution of 30-60 pc/cm^3 at an impact parameter of 50 kpc from the galaxy, declining to ~ 20 pc/cm^3 at the virial radius. These values are consistent with the 30-70 pc/cm^3 contribution of the Galactic halo inferred from FRB sightlines, while the dispersion in DM at fixed radius reflects the clumpiness of the gas. The CGM rotates with a velocity at about 0.5 of the disc rotation speed, and the rotation measure shows coherence over scales of about 10 kpc, consistent with the observed RM of |RM| ~ 10 rad/m^2.

Highly eccentric, short-period binaries pose a significant challenge for N-body integration in collisional codes because the time step must resolve pericentre passages, which dominates the computation cost. The slow-down time-transformed explicit symplectic integrator (TTL) of the algorithmic regularization family deals with the binary subsystem with a time transformation, which causes the time step to shrink near pericentre, while the secular evolution of the binary is followed with a slow-down factor kappa that scales the perturbation from the rest of the system, since the Keplerian motion is fast relative to the evolution of the binary orbital elements. This procedure reduces the number of steps for binaries with e > 0.99 and periods shorter than 10^-3 of the system crossing time by a factor of 100 while conserving the energy to a relative error of 10^-8.

The X/gamma-ray imaging spectrometer (XGIS) onboard THESEUS consists of two cameras with silicon drift detectors coupled to CsI scintillator bars, covering 2 keV to 10 MeV. The field of view is 2 sr at half sensitivity within the 2-30 keV band, with a coded-mask imaging capability providing an angular resolution of about 5 arcmin in the soft band. The energy resolution is 300 eV FWHM at 6 keV in the low-energy range and 18 percent at 100 keV for the CsI part. The effective area for the 2-30 keV band reaches 400 cm^2 on-axis, and peaks at about 1000 cm^2 in the 30 keV-1 MeV range for the combined detectors. The location accuracy for bright bursts is better than 15 arcmin, and the localisation is a few arcmin in the low-energy band.

Single-epoch black hole masses derived from H-beta carry a systematic dependence on the Fe II strength, R_Fe = EW(Fe II 4434-4684)/EW(H-beta), because strong Fe II sources tend to have high accretion rates and a narrower line profile for a given mass. Adding a correction term proportional to log R_Fe in the virial relation, with coefficient of about -0.3, lowers the masses of quasars with R_Fe > 1 by 0.2-0.4 dex relative to the uncorrected values. The fraction of sources accreting above the Eddington limit, with L_bol/L_Edd > 1, increases correspondingly, from about 5 percent to 15 percent. Conversely, quasars with weak Fe II receive higher masses, and the net effect on the overall distribution of M_BH is modest, with a median shift of 0.05 dex.

Stellar-mass black holes in X-ray binaries are weighed through dynamical measurements of the companion star's radial velocity curve, from which the mass function f(M) = P K^3/(2 pi G) = M_BH^3 sin^3 i/(M_BH+M_*)^2 follows, with the inclination determined from ellipticity of the light curve of the companion. For supermassive black holes in galactic nuclei, masses are measured with stellar dynamics (Schwarzschild modelling of the stellar kinematics), gas dynamics, megamaser disc rotation, and direct observation of stellar orbits in the Galactic Centre, which gives 4.3x10^6 Msun for Sgr A*. In active galaxies, the mass is estimated via reverberation mapping, which uses the time delay of the broad-line response to continuum variations and a virial factor f ~ 1-5 calibrated on the M-sigma relation.

We compare a one-dimensional radiative transfer code for a quasar's ionizing radiation with several three-dimensional Monte Carlo and ray-tracing codes for a standardized test problem: a quasar with a hard spectrum switching on in a uniform, initially neutral medium of density 10^-3 cm^-3. The 1D code reproduces the position of the H II ionization front to within 3 percent and the He III front within 5 percent for times up to 100 Myr, and the temperature profile behind the fronts, with T ~ 3x10^4 K inside the He III zone, agrees to 10 percent with the 3D codes. Differences are largest in the partially ionized front region where the hard photons yield pre-heating, and the 1D code is faster by a factor of 10^3, but it cannot capture anisotropic or clumpy media.

In the model where a black hole engine is fuelled by tidal disruptions of stars in a nuclear cluster, the predicted obscuration depends on the geometry of the debris. We compute the nuclear extinction for three configurations: a spherical shell, a thick torus and a thin disc with a scale height h/R of 0.1. For a rate of 10^-4 disruptions per year, the column density varies from N_H ~ 10^22 cm^-2 for spherical to 10^24 cm^-2 for the equatorial torus-like geometry, spanning two orders of magnitude, and so the fraction of obscured lines of sight is highly sensitive to the opening angle. The extinction A_V for a dust-to-gas ratio typical of the Milky Way varies from 5 to 500 mag. The predicted covering fraction between 0.3 and 0.9 reflects the geometry assumed.

The Higgsless approach models the scalar field of a first-order phase transition through a hydrodynamic description of the fluid alone, using a phenomenological model for the bubble wall as a source term, without evolving the Higgs-like order parameter explicitly. The bubble nucleates with a prescribed profile and the wall expands at a prescribed speed v_w, while the relativistic fluid is evolved with a conservative scheme, which permits much larger simulation volumes and a larger number of bubbles. The gravitational wave spectrum is computed from the fluid shear stress through the Green's function of the Einstein equation. Sound waves lasting for a Hubble time yield a peak frequency set by the mean bubble separation, f ~ 10 uHz for T_* ~ 100 GeV and beta/H_* ~ 10, with amplitude Omega_GW h^2 ~ 10^-10 for strong transitions with alpha ~ 0.3.

Millisecond pulsars with distances measured to better than 5 percent are rare, and the timing parallax, VLBI parallax and Shapiro delay combine to define a few of them as anchors. At nanohertz frequencies near 10 nHz the gravitational wave phase at the pulsar term is determined by the light travel time of order d/c, so to phase-coherently connect the pulsar and Earth terms, the distance must be known to a fraction of the gravitational wave wavelength of ~ 1 pc, which is far beyond precision currently achieved. The best candidates, PSR J0437-4715 at 156.98 +/- 0.15 pc, J0613-0200 and J1713+0747 with VLBI parallax uncertainties of 0.02 mas, have distance errors of 1-10 pc, which are good enough to be phase anchors for 10 nHz wave sources only in the best case of J0437.

Hydrodynamical simulations of dense star clusters need a prescription for collisions between stars, since resolving the merger product's structure in detail is computationally infeasible. We adopt a sticky-sphere approximation: two stars merge when their separation falls below the sum of their radii, and the product is a single particle with mass equal to the sum of the colliding masses minus a small mass loss fraction of 0.1 or less, with momentum conserved. The merger product is assumed to have the evolution of a star of the same mass on the main sequence, with its radius computed from a mass-radius relation and without rejuvenation or the consideration of entropy. This leads to errors in stellar radii of a factor of ~ 2 shortly after the collision, but has little effect over long times.

The spin temperature T_S of the 21-cm hyperfine transition describes the relative population of the triplet and singlet levels, and is the weighted mean of three temperatures: T_S^-1 = (T_CMB^-1 + x_c T_K^-1 + x_alpha T_alpha^-1)/(1 + x_c + x_alpha). Radiative coupling to the cosmic microwave background drives T_S towards T_CMB, collisions with atoms and electrons (x_c) drive it to the kinetic temperature T_K at high density, important at z > 50, and the Wouthuysen-Field effect, in which Lyman-alpha photons scattering off H I change the hyperfine state, couples T_S to the colour temperature of the Ly-alpha radiation, T_alpha ~ T_K. During cosmic dawn, the onset of star formation drives x_alpha above unity, and with T_K < T_CMB gives an absorption signal, followed by emission once X-ray heating takes over.

For gas of primordial composition to collapse into a supermassive star, cooling by molecular hydrogen must be suppressed, so that the gas remains at T ~ 8000 K, set by atomic hydrogen line cooling, and the Jeans mass is high, > 10^4 Msun. This can be accomplished by a strong Lyman-Werner background (J_21 > 10^3) photodissociating H2, by dynamical heating during rapid halo assembly, or by supersonic baryon streaming velocities relative to dark matter. In the atomic cooling halo of virial temperature > 10^4 K, gas collapses nearly isothermally with accretion rates of 0.1-1 Msun/yr, and fragmentation is limited by the lack of efficient cooling, and by the turbulence and gravitational torque which removes angular momentum. The resulting central protostar bloats to about 10^3 Rsun and grows into a supermassive star of 10^5 Msun.

We test whether an early dark energy component with an anti-de Sitter phase, which gives a negative contribution to the energy density at z ~ 2000 before the transition, combined with a low-redshift dynamical dark energy component of the w0wa type, can give a consistent fit to the Planck CMB, DESI BAO and SH0ES distance ladder datasets. The AdS phase raises H0 through the shortened sound horizon, and the best fit with H0 = 72.8 +/- 0.8 km/s/Mpc resolves the tension with SH0ES at the 1 sigma level. The DESI preference for phantom crossing, with w0 = -0.8 and wa = -0.8, is retained with the combined model. However, the chi-squared improvement relative to LCDM, Delta chi^2 ~ -25 for 6 additional parameters, is mostly driven by SH0ES, while the fit to the CMB damping tail and to the BAO data is slightly worse.

The JWST NIRSpec IFU spectrum of the z ~ 3 quasar shows complex broad-line profiles that require several Gaussian components. Paschen-beta is described by a broad component with FWHM = 4200 +/- 200 km/s and flux of 8x10^-17 erg/s/cm^2 and an intermediate component with FWHM = 1500 km/s and flux 3x10^-17 erg/s/cm^2, along with a narrow component of FWHM ~ 400 km/s. H-alpha is fitted with the same components, with FWHMs of 4300 and 1600 km/s and fluxes of 6x10^-16 and 2x10^-16 erg/s/cm^2. For H-beta, the broad component is FWHM = 4100 km/s with flux 1.5x10^-16, and the intermediate component is 1400 km/s with flux 7x10^-17, with the kinematic components tied across the lines. The broad-line ratio H-alpha/H-beta is 4, indicating moderate reddening.

The virial parameter alpha_vir = 5 sigma^2 R/(G M) determines the degree to which a dense gas cloud is bound, and affects the efficiency of the runaway stellar collisions that produce a very massive star. In clouds with alpha_vir < 1, collapse is rapid and the central stellar density increases quickly, so that the collision time falls below the stellar lifetime, and the very massive star grows via mergers to 10^3-10^4 Msun. In clouds with alpha_vir ~ 2, the collapse is slowed down and the star formation is spread over a larger region, resulting in more modest merger products with masses of order 10^2 Msun. The final mass scales approximately as alpha_vir^-1.5 in simulations with a cloud mass of 10^6 Msun, radius of 1 pc, and a star formation efficiency of 0.3.

The Egg, J1025+1402, is a local little red dot at z = 0.1, with a V-shaped spectral energy distribution displaying a turn-over near the rest-frame wavelength of 3646 A, a compact optical morphology with effective radius below 100 pc, and a red rest-optical continuum. The SDSS spectrum shows a broad H-alpha with FWHM ~ 2000 km/s, with a strong narrow Balmer absorption at the same velocity as the broad lines, and weak [O III]. The Balmer decrement of the broad lines is H-alpha/H-beta ~ 5, the black hole mass estimate is ~ 10^6.5-10^7 Msun with L_bol ~ 10^44 erg/s, and the X-ray emission is weak. The Egg offers nearby access for multi-wavelength follow-up of the little red dot population.

Little red dots are overwhelmingly undetected in X-rays, even in the deepest Chandra fields. Of the roughly 70 spectroscopically confirmed broad-line LRDs in the CDF-S, COSMOS and UDS fields, fewer than 5 percent have X-ray counterparts, and the stacked signal in the 0.5-8 keV band yields upper limits of L_X < 10^42.5 erg/s, which is one to two orders of magnitude below standard AGN scalings for their broad-line luminosities. The exceptions are a handful of brighter sources, such as lensed or relatively low-redshift objects at z < 3, where individual detections show hard spectra with L_2-10keV ~ 10^43-10^44 erg/s and moderate column densities of N_H ~ 10^23 cm^-2, and a candidate at z = 2.5 with strong variability, suggesting that X-ray weakness is not universal.

Several independent lines of evidence argue against LRDs being typical dust-obscured AGN. First, the spectral energy distribution shows a V-shaped continuum with a turn-over at the Balmer limit, and the flat rest-frame near-infrared slope with no hot-dust excess in MIRI photometry, which is inconsistent with the AGN torus emission expected for an A_V ~ 3 reddened quasar. Second, the far-infrared is not detected in ALMA continuum stacks, with dust masses below 10^7 Msun. Third, the sources are X-ray weak by more than an order of magnitude. Fourth, the broad Balmer lines display high Halpha/Hbeta decrements inconsistent with the A_V required by the optical continuum, and the lines are accompanied by Balmer breaks and absorption, pointing to dense gas instead of dust.

Fe II emission in LRDs is generally weak or absent, in contrast to the prominent optical Fe II pseudo-continuum in the 4434-4684 A and 5100-5400 A blends that is seen in many typical type 1 AGN, where R_Fe = EW(Fe II)/EW(H-beta) ~ 0.5-1. In the stacked NIRSpec spectra of LRDs, we find R_Fe < 0.1 at 3 sigma, and the UV Fe II complexes beneath Mg II 2800 are also not significantly detected. Where Fe II is observed, it appears in a few objects with narrow Fe II and Fe II lines in absorption, and an Fe II / Fe III ratio indicating very dense gas, n_H > 10^10 cm^-3. The weakness of Fe II is consistent with high-density gas, in which Fe II is collisionally quenched or the iron is depleted.

Resonant scattering and electron scattering shape the emission lines of LRDs through different channels. In the dense gas cloud surrounding the black hole, with N_H > 10^24 cm^-2, Lyman-alpha and the Balmer lines are subject to resonant scattering, which, because of the high optical depth in n=2 hydrogen, can create Balmer absorption and boost the strengths of the Balmer lines through collisional excitation and Lyman-alpha pumping. Electron scattering with an optical depth tau_e ~ 1-3 on thermal electrons of 10^4-10^5 K produces symmetric exponential line wings, with a width of order (kT/m_e c^2)^0.5 c ~ 1000-3000 km/s, thus explaining the Lorentzian-like line profiles without invoking rapid virial motions, and meaning that the black hole masses based on the FWHM may be overestimated by an order of magnitude.

We classify all NIRSpec PRISM spectra in the sample using a decision tree based on the continuum slope, the presence of a Balmer break, and the detection of broad Balmer emission lines. Sources with a blue rest-UV slope, a red rest-optical continuum with inflection near the Balmer limit, and broad H-alpha with FWHM > 1500 km/s are labelled little red dots (LRDs). Of 4,200 PRISM spectra at z > 3, 118 satisfy these criteria. Their spectral shapes are remarkably homogeneous, with a scatter of only 0.15 dex in the normalized continuum, suggesting that LRDs constitute a single, unified population of dust-reddened AGN rather than a heterogeneous mix of starbursts and obscured quasars.

We compute grids of nebular emission with the photoionization code Cloudy, adopting stellar population synthesis ionizing spectra (BPASS and Starburst99) and varying the gas-phase oxygen abundance from 12+log(O/H) = 7.0 to 9.2, the ionization parameter log U from -4 to -1, and the electron density. The models reproduce the star-forming sequence in the [N II]/H-alpha versus [O III]/H-beta diagram and are used to calibrate line-ratio diagnostics such as R23, O32, and N2O2. We also include models with enhanced N/O and with alpha-enhanced abundance patterns appropriate for high-redshift galaxies. The grids cover a wide metallicity range from 0.02 to 2 times solar and are interpolated to fit observed fluxes with a Bayesian scheme.

The Abell S1063 field was observed with NIRCam as part of a Cycle 2 Treasury program designed to reach ultra-deep imaging of a strong-lensing cluster. Eight broad- and medium-band filters from F090W to F444W reach 5 sigma depths of m_AB ~ 30.5 in the cluster core. Because of the lensing magnification, which exceeds a factor of 10 over a significant area, this imaging probes intrinsic UV absolute magnitudes fainter than M_UV = -14 at z ~ 6-9. The data are intended to constrain the faint end of the UV luminosity function and the contribution of faint galaxies to cosmic reionization. Parallel NIRCam observations of an adjacent blank field provide a control sample.

We fit the broadband SEDs of the high-redshift AGN sample with composite models including an AGN accretion disk, a host galaxy stellar population, and a dust screen applied separately to each component. We find a median AGN attenuation of A_V = 2.1 mag, while the host galaxy attenuation is only A_V = 0.6 mag. The AGN are therefore more heavily attenuated than their hosts by roughly 1.5 mag, implying that the obscuring dust is located close to the nucleus rather than distributed on galactic scales. Fits with a single common attenuation value yield significantly worse chi-squared values (Delta chi^2 > 30) and overpredict the rest-UV flux, indicating that the host contributes an unobscured blue component.

Anti-truncated, or Type III, surface brightness profiles are found in about 40 per cent of the dust-rich S0 galaxies in our sample, with a break radius at roughly 2.5 disc scale lengths and a shallower outer slope. The outer discs are bluer than the inner regions and show stellar ages of 3-5 Gyr, while the dust lanes are frequently misaligned with the stellar disc. These properties are consistent with a minor or intermediate-mass merger origin, in which accreted gas settles at large radii and forms stars after the primary disc has faded. We compare with N-body simulations of gas-rich mergers, which reproduce the break strength and the kinematic misalignment, and conclude that mergers are the most likely origin of anti-truncated profiles in dusty S0 galaxies.

Within the RUBIES spectroscopic survey we identify 63 broad-line AGN at 3 < z < 8, defined by a broad H-alpha component with FWHM > 1000 km/s at greater than 5 sigma significance. Of these, only 21 satisfy the photometric colour cuts and compactness criteria (F277W-F444W > 0.7, effective radius < 100 pc) used to define little red dots; the remaining 42 are either bluer, more extended, or both. The non-LRD broad-line sources span a wide range of black hole masses, 10^6.5 to 10^8.5 Msun, and show lower Balmer decrements on average. We discuss how colour- and size-based selection misses a considerable fraction of the broad-line population, and how the LRD sample compares with these AGN.

We follow the collapse of gas in 10^6 Msun minihalos using high-resolution cosmological zoom simulations that reach a mass resolution of 0.1 Msun per gas particle. The temperature-density relation shows a characteristic evolution: the gas first heats adiabatically to the virial temperature of about 1000 K at n ~ 1 cm^-3, then cools through H2 line emission to roughly 200 K at n ~ 10^4 cm^-3, close to the temperature minimum set by the H2 level populations. At n > 10^8 cm^-3, three-body H2 formation drives a rise in temperature to ~1000 K, and collisional-induced emission becomes important. The scatter in temperature at fixed density depends on the halo assembly history and the strength of the Lyman-Werner background.

In dense star-forming clouds at cosmic dawn, with surface densities above 10^3 Msun pc^-2, the escape velocity at the cloud radius exceeds ~50 km/s. The momentum injected by stellar winds and by direct radiation pressure is insufficient to unbind the gas, because the ratio of the feedback force to the gravitational weight is below unity, and HII regions are quenched as the free-fall time becomes shorter than the time required for stars to inject sufficient energy. Supernovae only begin after ~3 Myr, by which time a large fraction of the gas has already been converted into stars. As a result the star formation efficiency can reach 50 per cent or higher, enabling the very efficient bursts and the formation of bound clusters inferred at high redshift.

We measure the local galaxy overdensity around spectroscopically confirmed little red dots using the NIRCam photometric redshift catalogs, counting neighbors within a projected radius of 1 pMpc and |dz| < 0.3. Relative to a control sample of galaxies matched in stellar mass and redshift, LRDs reside in environments of lower density: the median overdensity is delta = -0.2 compared with delta = +0.3 for the control galaxies at 3 < z < 10. The number of companions within 100 kpc is consistent with that of the field, and no excess of massive neighbours is found. These results indicate that LRDs do not preferentially occupy the densest regions of the cosmic web and are therefore unlikely to be hosted by the most massive halos.

We select dust-obscured galaxies (DOGs) with a mid-infrared excess, requiring a ratio of 24 micron to R-band flux density greater than 1000, and identify a WISE counterpart in the W4 band at 22 micron. The surface density of WISE-detected DOGs with S_22 > 5 mJy is 0.03 deg^-2, compared to 0.12 deg^-2 for optically luminous type 1 quasars at the same mid-infrared flux limit. The integral source counts show a steeper slope for the DOGs, with dN/dS proportional to S^-2.6, indicating that obscured sources become more common than unobscured ones below ~3 mJy. The ratio of DOGs to type 1 quasars is therefore near 0.3 at the bright end and rises to above unity at fainter fluxes.

For a star orbiting a massive black hole in a power-law stellar cusp with density rho proportional to r^-gamma, the extended mass of the cusp induces a retrograde precession of the pericenter that opposes the prograde Schwarzschild precession. The mass precession timescale is t_M = P (M_bh / M_*(<a)) / sqrt(1 - e^2) up to a factor of order unity depending on gamma, where P is the orbital period and M_*(<a) is the enclosed stellar mass within the semimajor axis a. For a cusp with gamma = 1.75 around a 4 x 10^6 Msun black hole, this gives t_M of about 10^6 yr at 0.1 pc. The competition between mass precession and relativistic precession sets the critical radius where resonant relaxation is quenched.

We derive the black hole mass function of SDSS broad-line quasars at 0.3 < z < 2 using single-epoch virial masses from H-beta, Mg II, and C IV, and correct for selection incompleteness using the survey selection function derived from simulated quasar spectra. After accounting for the magnitude limit and the host galaxy, the number density per dex in log M_BH peaks near 10^8 Msun and declines steeply above 10^9.5 Msun. The mass function is constrained down to log(M_BH/Msun) = 7.5 at z ~ 0.5 and to 8.3 at z ~ 2, below which the incompleteness corrections exceed a factor of 3, and the shape depends on the assumed Eddington ratio distribution. The uncertainty is dominated by the 0.4 dex scatter in virial masses.

Stacking X-ray Chandra data for more than 100 little red dots yields no detection, with a 3 sigma upper limit on the rest-frame 2-10 keV luminosity of L_X < 10^42.5 erg/s, nearly two orders of magnitude below the value expected from the broad H-alpha luminosities for typical AGN. Three explanations have been proposed. First, the AGN may be intrinsically X-ray weak, for example if they accrete at super-Eddington rates with a geometrically thick inner disk that shields the corona. Second, a column density above 10^24 cm^-2 could absorb the soft X-rays. Third, broad H-alpha may be produced by electron scattering or by outflows rather than by virial motion, so black hole masses and luminosities would be overestimated.

We compare the kinematics of the broad-line region and the narrow-line region in blue quasars at z ~ 2, using C IV and [O III] 5007 measured from near-infrared spectra. In non-BAL quasars, the C IV blueshift correlates with the [O III] blue wing velocity, v_10 ~ -800 km/s, while in BAL quasars the [O III] outflow velocities, v_10 ~ -1200 km/s, are systematically higher by approximately 400 km/s, and the C IV emission lines are strongly blueshifted by 2000-3000 km/s. Despite the similar bolometric luminosities (log L_bol ~ 46.5) and Eddington ratios, BAL quasars show broader [O III] profiles with FWHM of 1800 km/s versus 1200 km/s. This suggests that BAL outflows are accompanied by more powerful large-scale winds.

We present a catalog of spectral measurements for 750,414 quasars from the SDSS Data Release 16 quasar catalog. For each object we fit the continuum, the iron emission templates, and the emission lines of H-alpha, H-beta, Mg II, and C IV with multi-Gaussian models, and provide line fluxes, equivalent widths, FWHM, line dispersion, and the corresponding uncertainties. Virial black hole masses are computed from H-beta, Mg II, and C IV with standard single-epoch calibrations, together with bolometric luminosities and Eddington ratios. The catalog also includes the host-corrected luminosity at 5100 Angstrom for sources with z < 0.8 and flags for broad absorption lines and bad fits. The catalogue is available as a FITS table in the online material.

We describe a Monte Carlo ionization and radiative transfer code for modeling the radiation and line formation in accretion disk winds. The code follows photon packets through a three-dimensional, axisymmetric biconical outflow, computing the ionization state, heating and cooling in a self-consistent iterative scheme, and includes bound-bound, bound-free and electron scattering opacities, with macro-atom treatment of the line transfer. We use the code to calculate synthetic UV spectra of BAL quasars and cataclysmic variables. The code is parallelized with MPI, is written in Python and C, and is publicly available under an open-source license, with documented examples and a set of precomputed atomic data.

In the early cooling flows in the progenitors of massive galaxies, the gas pressure is high, with P/k_B exceeding 10^7 K cm^-3 owing to the deep potential wells and the high accretion rates at z ~ 3-5. The Jeans mass in this dense, warm medium is lower than in typical Milky Way clouds, M_J ~ 0.1 Msun, so fragmentation produces a larger fraction of low-mass stars, resulting in a bottom-heavy initial mass function with a slope steeper than Salpeter below 0.5 Msun. Models in which the characteristic mass scales with the thermal Jeans mass predict that the IMF becomes bottom-heavy in the highest pressure environments, consistent with the elevated mass-to-light ratios and dwarf-sensitive spectral features observed in massive early-type galaxies.

We examine decade-long optical light curves of J1047+0739, a local analog of the high-redshift little red dots, using archival photometry from the Zwicky Transient Facility, Pan-STARRS, and the Catalina Real-time Transient Survey, covering 2009-2024. The light curve shows no significant variability: the excess variance is consistent with zero, sigma_rms < 0.05 mag, and no coherent trends are found on timescales from days to years. The structure function is flat at all lags, in contrast to the typical AGN damped random walk behaviour of luminous quasars with similar luminosity. This lack of optical variability is consistent with the findings for high-redshift little red dots, and it may suggest a dense gas envelope smoothing the intrinsic variability from the central accretion disk.

We construct empirical SED templates for luminous quasars by combining photometry from the UV to the mid-infrared of 2,500 spectroscopically confirmed QSOs from SDSS, 2MASS, and WISE. The sample is divided into unobscured type 1 and obscured quasars on the basis of the optical-to-mid-infrared colour r - W4 and the presence of broad lines. We provide mean templates in bins of bolometric luminosity, from 10^45 to 10^47 erg/s, along with the corresponding SED scatter. The obscured templates are reddened relative to the unobscured ones, with a stronger 10 micron silicate feature and a mid-infrared bump peaking at 15 micron. The templates are tabulated from 0.1 to 100 microns and can be used directly for photometric fitting of AGN and photometric redshift estimation.

For unreddened blue AGN, the intrinsic broad-line Balmer decrement is found to be H-alpha/H-beta = 3.1 +/- 0.3, slightly above the Case B recombination value of 2.86, because of collisional excitation and radiative transfer effects in the high-density (n_H ~ 10^10-10^11 cm^-3) gas of the broad-line region. Using a sample of 5,000 SDSS quasars selected to have blue continua (alpha_nu > -0.5) and no narrow absorption, we measure a median decrement of 3.06, with an intrinsic scatter of 0.4. Adopting the value of 2.86 therefore overestimates the dust reddening by E(B-V) ~ 0.03 mag for broad lines, which is important when estimating the attenuation of high-redshift sources.

The efficiency of long gamma-ray burst production per unit star formation is found to increase toward low metallicity, with the fraction of massive stars producing GRBs being higher by a factor of 5-10 below 0.3 solar metallicity, as expected from collapsar models requiring rapid rotation of the progenitor. The cosmic GRB rate density follows the star formation history only if this metallicity bias is included, with a mild redshift evolution of the GRB-to-SFR ratio proportional to (1+z)^1.2. At z > 6, where the UV luminosity density measured by JWST exceeds the extrapolation of the pre-JWST models, GRBs offer an unbiased probe, since the afterglows are visible regardless of the host brightness, and could test whether the apparent star formation excess is real.

The blue companion near the lensed little red dot lies at a projected separation of 0.4 kpc and has a spectrum with strong [O III] and narrow Balmer lines, but no broad components, implying a star-forming or photoionized origin. We consider whether it could be a clump of metal-enriched gas ejected from the red AGN component by an outflow. The gas-phase metallicity of 12+log(O/H) = 8.3 is high for the host's mass and is similar to that of the AGN broad-line region. With an outflow velocity of ~600 km/s, the gas would travel 0.4 kpc in 0.7 Myr, which is shorter than the lifetime of the AGN phase, so such an ejection scenario is dynamically viable.

The fundamental plane of black hole activity relates the 5 GHz radio luminosity, the 2-10 keV X-ray luminosity, and the black hole mass: log L_R = 0.6 log L_X + 0.78 log M_BH + 7.3, with an intrinsic scatter of 0.4 dex, originally calibrated for low-luminosity and hard-state accreting black holes. For radio-quiet AGN at z up to 4, the correlation is found with a similar slope but a lower normalization, offset by 1.5-2 dex from that of radio-loud sources, with the X-ray emitting corona and the radio-emitting region being coupled. We use a sample of 400 radio-quiet AGN from deep VLA and Chandra surveys, and find that the relation does not evolve with redshift within the uncertainties.

To cross-identify FIRST radio sources with SDSS optical counterparts, we adopt a matching radius of 2 arcsec. At this radius the completeness for point-like radio sources is about 95 per cent, while the fraction of random associations is below 1 per cent, as estimated by shifting the radio positions by 1 arcmin and repeating the matching. Increasing the radius to 5 arcsec raises the completeness only marginally for core-dominated sources, but increases the false-match fraction to over 8 per cent, given the surface density of about 100 optical sources per square degree at i < 20. For extended double-lobed sources, we use a separate procedure based on the radio morphology and the position of the radio core.

Electron temperatures are derived from the Balmer jump, T_e(BJ), by measuring the discontinuity at 3646 Angstrom relative to the adjacent H11-H15 emission lines, and from the Paschen jump at 8204 Angstrom, with typical values of 12,000-18,000 K in low-metallicity galaxies. These continuum-based temperatures tend to be lower than those based on [O III] 4363/5007, owing to temperature fluctuations. The Balmer jump is degenerate with the nebular continuum fraction and with dust attenuation, because reddening changes the observed slope across the jump. A Bayesian fit, combining the Balmer jump, the Paschen jump, and the Balmer decrement and imposing a prior on E(B-V), reduces the degeneracy but leaves an uncertainty of about 1500 K.

To identify quasars suitable for helium II absorption studies, we selected objects that are bright in the far-ultraviolet by cross-matching the GALEX GR5 catalogue with the SDSS DR7 quasar sample. We required a FUV magnitude brighter than 21 AB, a redshift 2.7 < z < 3.5 so that the He II Lyman-alpha forest at 304 Angstrom falls above the GALEX FUV cutoff at 1350 Angstrom, and no strong intervening Lyman limit systems in the SDSS spectrum. The resulting candidates were vetted by visual inspection and by comparing the NUV and FUV colours, yielding 25 targets of which 11 were observed with HST/COS. Sightlines with a high FUV flux are rare, since the He II optical depth is high at z > 2.8.

The positions of the ISO 15 micron sources were corrected for astrometric offsets caused by glitches in the pointing reconstruction and, in lensed fields, by the displacement between the lensed images and the cluster. We cross-correlated the ISOCAM source positions with a reference optical catalogue, derived the systematic shift for each raster, and applied a global correction, which reduced the rms residual from 4 arcsec to 1.2 arcsec. Sources with a pixel-to-pixel glitch signature, identified with the Multiresolution Median Transform method, were flagged and either removed or re-extracted. The final catalogue contains 600 sources above 100 microJy, with a positional accuracy of about 1.5 arcsec, which enables reliable identification with optical and near-infrared counterparts.

The broad O I 8446 emission line in Seyfert 1 galaxies can be excited by Lyman-beta fluorescence, in which H I Lyman-beta photons at 1025.7 Angstrom pump the O I 3d 3D level, by collisional excitation in a high-density, partially ionized zone, or by recombination. These processes can be distinguished by the line ratio to O I 11287, which is approximately 1 for fluorescent excitation, and to O I 13165, which is strongly enhanced by collisional excitation. Photoionization models with density n_H = 10^11 cm^-3 and ionization parameter log U = -2 reproduce the observed 8446/11287 ratio of 1.2 for most objects in our sample. A stronger 8446 line compared to Ca II triplet suggests Lyman-beta fluorescence is dominant.

From a mid-infrared selection of quasars with S_24 > 0.3 mJy and a high ratio of 24 micron to optical flux (R - [24] > 14), we estimate the ratio of obscured to unobscured quasars at z > 1. After correcting for the incompleteness of the optical selection of type 1 quasars and for the contribution of star-forming galaxies to the 24 micron population, we find that the ratio is approximately 2:1 for luminosities log L_bol > 45.5 and rises to 3:1 at lower luminosities. The obscured fraction is thus about 65-75 per cent, in agreement with the predictions of unification models in which the covering fraction of the torus decreases with luminosity, and with the results from X-ray surveys. The uncertainty is dominated by the spectroscopic incompleteness.

Ultradeep mid-infrared imaging of the Hubble Ultra Deep Field and the GOODS-South field was obtained with the IRAC camera aboard Spitzer, combining several programs. The GOODS Legacy program provided 3.6, 4.5, 5.8, and 8.0 micron data to a depth of about 23.5 hr per pixel, while the IRAC Ultradeep Field (IUDF) and the S-CANDELS survey added an additional ~100 hr at 3.6 and 4.5 microns over the UDF and surrounding region. The Spitzer Extended Deep Survey and the GREATS program contributed further coverage. The combined mosaics reach 5 sigma limiting magnitudes of 27.0 AB at 3.6 micron and are used to constrain the stellar masses of galaxies at z > 6.

To remove the host galaxy starlight from SDSS AGN spectra, we use a principal component analysis decomposition, in which each spectrum is fitted as a linear combination of galaxy eigenspectra, derived from a sample of 170,000 galaxies without AGN signatures, and quasar eigenspectra derived from high-luminosity quasars. The number of eigenspectra is set to ten for the galaxy and to five for the quasar, and the best-fitting coefficients are obtained by minimizing chi-squared in the rest-frame wavelength range 3500-7000 Angstrom, with emission-line regions masked. The reconstructed host spectrum is then subtracted from the observed data, leaving the AGN continuum and the broad lines. Tests with simulated spectra show that the host fraction at 4200 Angstrom is recovered to within 10 per cent.

The effects of rotation are incorporated into the one-dimensional stellar structure equations by averaging over isobaric surfaces, which are no longer spherical in a rotating star, under the assumption of shellular rotation, where the angular velocity is constant on isobars. The equations of hydrostatic equilibrium and radiative transport are modified by correction factors f_P and f_T that depend on the ratio of the centrifugal force to gravity, and the effective gravity is lowered by the term (2/3) Omega^2 r. Transport of angular momentum is treated by an advection-diffusion equation, taking into account meridional circulation and shear instabilities, while chemical species are mixed by a diffusion coefficient D_eff. These modifications are implemented in the stellar evolution code at each timestep.

We reconstruct the intrinsic Lyman-alpha emission profile of the z = 7.5 quasar by fitting a principal component analysis model, trained on a sample of 13,000 low-redshift quasars from SDSS and HST observations, which predicts the continuum blueward of the Lyman-alpha line from the red side of the spectrum (1280-2850 Angstrom). The typical uncertainty of the predicted continuum is 10 per cent. We then divide the observed spectrum by the reconstructed continuum to obtain the transmission profile, and fit it with a model of the IGM damping wing that depends on the volume-averaged neutral hydrogen fraction x_HI and on the quasar lifetime. The measured damping wing implies x_HI ~ 0.4 at z = 7.5 with a 68 per cent interval of 0.2-0.6.

The confusion noise produced by the unresolved Galactic white-dwarf binaries is modeled by generating a synthetic population of 3 x 10^7 double white dwarfs, with a spatial distribution following the disc and bulge of the Milky Way, and computing the strain amplitude for each system at LISA frequencies of 0.1-10 mHz. Binaries with a signal-to-noise ratio above 7 are considered resolved and subtracted iteratively, and the remaining unresolved signal is added to the instrument noise as an effective spectral density S_c(f) = 1.8 x 10^-44 f^(-7/3) exp(-f^alpha + beta f sin(kappa f)) [1 + tanh(gamma (f_k - f))] Hz^-1, with fit parameters that depend on the mission duration. The confusion noise dominates the sensitivity between 0.3 and 3 mHz.

For counterparts to the unassociated Fermi gamma-ray sources, optical spectra were obtained with the 8-m Gemini and VLT telescopes. Redshifts were measured from narrow emission lines, such as [O II], [O III], and H-alpha, or from absorption features of the host galaxy for BL Lac candidates. For featureless spectra, where the continuum dominates, we derived lower limits on the redshift from the detection of intervening absorption systems, in particular the Mg II doublet at 2796 and 2803 Angstrom, assuming that the source lies behind the absorber. For 14 of the 45 BL Lac objects we obtained z > 0.5 limits in this way, with a rest-frame equivalent width threshold of 0.3 Angstrom. The typical S/N of the spectra is 30 per pixel.

Among the many properties of Green Pea galaxies investigated, including stellar mass, star formation rate, metallicity, dust attenuation, ionization parameter, and [O III]/[O II] ratio, we find that the Lyman-alpha escape fraction and the equivalent width correlate most strongly with the dust attenuation E(B-V), with a Spearman coefficient of rho = -0.72, followed by the [O III]/[O II] ratio and the velocity separation of the Lyman-alpha peaks. Galaxies with low extinction (E(B-V) < 0.1) have escape fractions of 20-40 per cent and Lyman-alpha equivalent widths above 40 Angstrom, while those with E(B-V) > 0.3 have escape fractions below 5 per cent. The correlation with metallicity is weaker and mostly driven by the dust content.

In the semi-analytic model, the metal yield is defined as the mass of metals ejected by a stellar population per unit mass locked into long-lived stars, and is set to y = 0.03 for a Chabrier IMF. We adopt the instantaneous recycling approximation, in which the stars more massive than 8 Msun die immediately after formation, returning a fraction R = 0.43 of their mass to the interstellar medium, together with newly synthesized metals. For the cold gas disc, the change in metallicity per star formation event is dZ_cold = y (1 - R) dm_star / m_cold, and the metals are mixed instantaneously and uniformly. A fraction of the metals is deposited directly into the hot halo gas by supernova-driven outflows, rather than the cold disc.

We forecast the constraints that the future LIGO/Virgo network at design sensitivity and the third-generation detectors could place on the fraction of dark matter in primordial black holes, f_PBH, by comparing the stochastic gravitational-wave background from unresolved mergers with the astrophysical background from stellar-mass binary black holes. Using a Fisher matrix analysis with the spectral shape of the energy density Omega_GW(f) ~ f^(2/3), the sensitivity of Omega_GW ~ 10^-10 after five years of observations at design sensitivity would limit f_PBH < 10^-3 for a 30 Msun monochromatic mass function, if the local merger rate is known to within a factor of 2. The constraints are degraded by degeneracy with the astrophysical redshift evolution of the merger rate.

We measure the sizes of Lyman-alpha emitters at z ~ 3 using HST/WFC3 imaging and find a median half-light radius of r_e = 0.9 kpc, with a typical stellar mass of 10^8.5 Msun. The LAEs are smaller than the extrapolation of the size-mass relation of more massive star-forming galaxies at the same redshift, by about 0.2-0.3 dex at a fixed stellar mass, lying below the relation measured for Lyman break galaxies with M_* > 10^9.5 Msun, r_e ~ r_0 (M_*/5 x 10^10)^0.2. The compact sizes imply high star-formation-rate surface densities, Sigma_SFR ~ 1-10 Msun/yr/kpc^2, which could favour the escape of Lyman-alpha photons through feedback-driven outflows.

For self-gravitating accretion disks in which mass is depleted by embedded stars, the accretion rate declines with decreasing radius, Mdot(r) proportional to r^alpha with alpha > 0. Since the disk must remain marginally stable at Toomre Q ~ 1, the surface density and viscous heating are set by the local condition, and the effective temperature follows T_eff^4 proportional to Mdot Omega^2 ~ r^(alpha - 3). For a sufficiently steep depletion, alpha approaches 3, giving a nearly flat T_eff profile of about 10^4 K, in contrast to the standard r^(-3/4) profile. The bolometric luminosity is dominated by the outer radius, since the emitting area grows as r^2, and the disc spectrum becomes a quasi-blackbody with a temperature close to the outer edge value.

We perform a suite of hydrodynamic simulations of a black hole embedded in a turbulent molecular cloud to test the dependence of runaway hyper-Eddington growth on the initial conditions. We vary the black hole's initial position (offset from the cloud centre by 0-5 pc), the initial velocity (0-30 km/s relative to the gas), and the gas metallicity (10^-3 to 1 solar). The accretion rate exceeds 1000 times the Eddington rate in all cases where the black hole is bound to the cloud. The growth is only mildly sensitive to the initial position and velocity once the black hole sinks to the dense region within a free-fall time, and it does not depend significantly on the metallicity, because the radiative feedback is trapped by the dense flow.

We fit the UV-to-infrared photometry of the heavily dust-reddened quasars at z ~ 2 with a model composed of an accretion disc component with a power-law slope alpha_lambda = -1.5, a Small Magellanic Cloud type dust extinction law with E(B-V) of 0.5-2.0 mag, a host galaxy stellar population from the BC03 library, and a hot dust and torus component fitted by a blackbody with T_dust ~ 1200 K. The best-fitting models require a significant host contribution in the optical and near-infrared bands, which comprises 30-50 per cent of the flux at 1 micron rest frame. The mid-infrared emission, 3-10 micron, is dominated by the AGN torus, with L_MIR ~ 10^46 erg/s, and the reddened accretion disc is reproduced with a chi-squared per degree of freedom near unity.

We measure the mean transmission of the IGM in the rest-frame wavelength range 1220-1260 Angstrom blueward of the Lyman-alpha break, <T_Lya>, in stacked JWST NIRSpec PRISM spectra of galaxies. The mean transmission declines with redshift, from about 0.55 at z = 5.5-6.0 to 0.20 at z ~ 7, and below 0.05 at z > 8, which is steeper than predicted by models of late reionization alone. The damping wing profile constrains the neutral fraction, x_HI ~ 0.3 at z = 7 and x_HI ~ 0.6 at z = 8. Comparison with reionization simulations shows good agreement with models in which reionization ends at z ~ 5.3, with an average mean free path of less than 10 cMpc.

In the wide JWST surveys, we find that the stellar mass function of the quiescent, early-type galaxies has a different shape from that of the star-forming, late-type galaxies at 1 < z < 4. The late-type galaxies are described by a Schechter function with a low-mass slope alpha = -1.4 and a characteristic mass log M* = 10.8, while early-types show a shallower slope, alpha ~ -0.3, with a turnover below 10^9.5 Msun and an exponential cutoff at a similar mass. The relative contribution of early-type galaxies to the total mass function increases with decreasing redshift, from 10 per cent at z ~ 3 to 40 per cent at z ~ 1 for stellar masses above 10^10.5 Msun. The shapes differ significantly out to z ~ 4.

We carry out Bayesian analyses of the pulsar timing array data using the parallel-tempering Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler PTMCMCSampler, with the signal models implemented in the enterprise package. The pulsar noise model for each of 67 pulsars includes white noise parameters EFAC, EQUAD, and ECORR for each backend, red noise modeled as a power law with 30 Fourier frequencies, and dispersion measure variations. The common-spectrum process, representing the gravitational-wave background, is described with 14 frequency bins, with the Hellings-Downs correlations. New-physics signals, including cosmic strings and phase transitions, are fitted using spectral templates in ceffyl, and Bayes factors are computed using the product-space method.

The merging Lyman break galaxy at z ~ 7 comprises two compact starbursting components separated by 1.2 kpc, with half-light radii of 150 pc. The SED fitting of the NIRCam and ALMA data indicates specific star formation rates of sSFR ~ 40 Gyr^-1 for the northern component and 25 Gyr^-1 for the southern one, corresponding to star formation rates of 30 and 20 Msun/yr and stellar masses of 7 x 10^8 and 8 x 10^8 Msun. The specific star formation rates are well above the main sequence at this redshift, implying a mass doubling time of 25-40 Myr, and are consistent with a merger-triggered starburst. The star-formation surface density is Sigma_SFR ~ 200 Msun/yr/kpc^2.

We investigate whether the choice of radial binning biases the halo concentrations derived from NFW fits to the density profiles of simulated dark matter haloes. Using linear bins in radius gives more weight to the outer parts of the halo and biases the concentration high by 10-20 per cent, while logarithmic bins with a fixed number of bins per dex weight the inner profile more strongly. The fits are also sensitive to the innermost radius, which we vary between the convergence radius of 0.01 R_vir and 0.05 R_vir, and to the number of bins (10-50).
